name: The agent entity checklist
lead: Everything an agent entity needs, whatever it becomes: an agent employee, an app, an open-source project or a company. Categories are questions every entity must answer; components are what you choose or build to answer them; elements are single decisions, each with the leading open-source option, the leading closed-source option and a default pick.

levels.layer: A group of categories that share one relation to the entity (the entity itself, how it meets the world, and so on).
levels.category: One question every entity must answer, such as 'What is it made of?'. The buckets never change with what the entity becomes.
levels.component: One thing you choose or build to answer the question, such as Memory.
levels.element: One decision inside a component, such as the long-term memory store. Each element names the open-source leader, the closed-source leader and a default pick.

columns.open: The leading option whose code anyone can run, with its evidence.
columns.closed: The leading hosted or enterprise option, with its evidence. Where neither side has a real option, the cell says why.
columns.pick: The default an entity gets when nobody chooses, and why. A pick is a default, not a lock: every row that names an alternative can be switched to it.

priorities.P0: From day one, for every entity.
priorities.P1: As soon as it serves people or other agents.
priorities.P2: Once it earns money or becomes a company.
priorities.P3: At scale, once the work proves the need.
priorities.P4: Owning the layers below the waterline: chips, buildings and power. Only when the work has proved it for years.

groups.name: The entity itself
groups.what: What it thinks with and what it is made of.

groups.name: How it meets the world
groups.what: Where it can be reached and what it works through, the doors people and agents use, what those doors are built from, and the other agents it works with.

groups.name: How it stays trusted, running and improving
groups.what: Why it is safe to rely on, how it is kept running, and how it gets better on its own.

groups.name: The business around it
groups.what: Money in and out, how people find it, who stands behind it, the legal body it lives in, and who pays until it pays for itself.

groups.name: Below the waterline
groups.what: Owning the compute: priorities 3 and 4, only after the product is proven.

identity.lead: Identity grew into four different things, which is why it became confusing. The self is who it is; its addresses are where it can be reached; proof is how anyone verifies who it is and whom it acts for; its standing is what it holds and answers for in its own name. Each has one home in the checklist.

kinds.name: The self
kinds.question: Who is it?
items: Grade, which sets its compute and spending caps

kinds.name: Its addresses
kinds.question: Where can people and agents reach it?
items: Email inbox, phone number and SMS

kinds.name: Proof
kinds.question: How does anyone know it is this agent, acting for this person?
items: An account in the customer's directory
Scoped keys held by a keeper, never by the agent

kinds.name: Its standing
kinds.question: What can it hold and answer for in its own name?
items: A bank account, and a card with a hard cap
A wallet, only when a customer pays in stablecoins or an employee trades
The company it works for, or becomes
A tax number, which needs a named person

identity.rule: Own the self; rent the addresses. An address can be swapped in a week; the corrections behind the self took a year. Standing always runs through a named person: a US tax number and a bank's identity check both need one.
identity.footer: Not identity: the computer, browser and connectors it works through (Reach) and the controls on it (Trust). Other agents reach it through its doors under Surfaces: its MCP server and its agent card. Some services set up one agent's accounts with one command and bundle pieces of all of these for one owner; the checklist names the underlying provider for each, so any one can be swapped.

access.lead: For each product a pick names: one column per way an agent can use it on its own, easiest first, then two properties that are not ways to act but make every route work better. Each tick links to its proof, read on the date shown; a column that does not apply says so.

remote_mcp.name: Hosted MCP
remote_mcp.means: The vendor runs an MCP server (Model Context Protocol) at a public address; an agent adds the address and signs in, with nothing to install.
remote_mcp.why: First, because it reaches the most agents with the least setup: chat apps with no command line (ChatGPT apps, Claude connectors) can only add tools this way, every coding agent can too, and each sign-in is per user and can be revoked.

cli.name: CLI
cli.means: An official command-line tool the agent installs and runs, ideally with JSON output.
cli.why: Second: where the agent has a command line it is the cheapest and most reliable route, since nothing loads into its context up front and the model often knows the tool already. It ranks below hosted MCP only because it needs a command line and a key in the agent's environment. For agents that always have a command line, it is the first route in daily use.

skill.name: Skill
skill.means: The vendor publishes Agent Skills: folders with a SKILL.md that teach an agent to use its CLI, API or MCP server, loaded only when a task needs them.
skill.why: Third: 46 agent clients read skills and a skill costs only its name until used, but it is the manual for the other routes, not a way to act on its own.

api.name: API or SDK
api.means: A documented, self-serve web API with keys, and the vendor's own client libraries.
api.why: Fourth: universal, and what the other routes are built from, but the agent must write the code and handle keys, paging and errors itself.

local_mcp.name: Local MCP
local_mcp.means: An MCP server the agent's machine installs and runs (with npx, uvx or Docker), with the key in its environment: the vendor's own package earns a full tick, a community-made one half.
local_mcp.why: Fifth, below the plain API: it wraps the same API in an extra process that must start and stay up; in a random sample of 400 servers from a registry census only 48.8% finished the MCP handshake.

computer.name: Computer use
computer.means: The agent drives the vendor's web app or console through screenshots, clicks and typing.
computer.why: Last, and never scored: it works on almost anything with a screen, so a tick says little. It is the slowest route (the best score on the OSWorld-Verified benchmark was 86.1% on 24 September 2026) and puts stored logins within reach of planted instructions.

docs.name: Docs for agents
docs.means: The vendor publishes an llms.txt file (checked to answer with text) or Markdown copies of its docs, so an agent reads only the page it needs.
docs.why: A property, not a way to act: it raises the success of every route, so it carries a small weight.

setup.name: Sets itself up
setup.means: After at most one sign-up by a person, the agent creates what it needs (an inbox, a number, a project, more credit) through the API, CLI or MCP.
setup.why: Running many entities depends on it: hundreds of entities means no portal clicks per entity. A registration every provider must require (US texting registration, an identity check) is noted, never held against one vendor.

rules: Access, 30%: the points of every column the pick ticks (hosted MCP 30, CLI 20, skill 15, API 15, local MCP 5, computer use 0, docs for agents 5, sets itself up 10), a partial tick counting half; a column that does not apply is left out, and a column not verified counts as a cross.
Adoption, 25%: how widely the players use it now, read from numbers (weekly downloads, stars, named customers, revenue) into a tier: leader 100, strong 75, growing 50, niche 25.

Quality, 20%: the mean of the quality checks that have a public source (a hands-on trial, a probe that its hosted MCP server answers or refuses correctly, a public benchmark); pass-or-fail checks alone are capped at 80, because passing shows a tool works, not how well.
Cost, 15%: free to start 100, low 80, mid 55, high 30, sales-led 15.
A part without evidence is left out and the weights are rescaled over the rest, never guessed. A row is scored only when access and at least three other parts are known; otherwise it says unscored.
The score compares products; it does not choose. Where a pick is not the product with the most ticks, its row says why.
Scores are rounded to the nearest whole number, a half to the even one (42.5 shows as 42).

notes: Data is not a category of its own, because each kind has one home: the customer's data comes through connectors (Reach), what the entity knows is Memory (Harness), the pool of verified cases is Evolution, and rights over data are Privacy (Trust).

Harness holds the eleven components of an agent's harness. Reachability sits under Reach; trust is a category of its own; self-improvement is the Evolution category; model routing is Routing under Intelligence.

Marketing is the Growth category: finding and keeping customers. Product analytics sits under Evolution as a signal, because its first job is telling the product what to fix; Growth reads the same numbers for funnels and retention.

The vertical (health care, law, finance) changes what fills each box, never the boxes. So does the kind of entity: an open-source project needs no company or funding round, but it still answers every question.
Outside the US the buckets hold; element names give the US form as the example (EIN, state registration, SOC 2, HIPAA, sales tax), and the local form fills the same box.
Some elements have no open-source option at all (a state filing, a bank, a card network). The cell says so, and the element stays swappable between vendors.
Evidence ages. Stars, prices and funding were read on the date in each product's record; read them again before a purchase.

categories.name: Intelligence
categories.question: What thinks and decides for it?
categories.what: The models it rents, and later the small ones it trains. Rented from day one; trained only on verified cases it has the right to keep.

components.name: Thinking
components.what: The frontier model: reads, plans, writes and handles what nobody has seen before.

elements.name: Frontier model
elements.what: The strongest general model, kept for judgement and new cases.
elements.open: Open-weight leaders on the Artificial Analysis index: Xiaomi MiMo-V2.6-Pro (46), GLM-5.3 (45), Kimi K3 (44); DeepSeek V4, Qwen3.8
elements.closed: Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 (58, first of 173 models), then OpenAI GPT-6 Astra (53)
elements.pick: Claude Code's default flagship (Opus 5.5 today), never a pinned model ID
elements.why: First on the independent index on 27 September 2026. Fable scores lower (53) at a higher price.

components.name: Deciding
components.what: Fast typed answers (yes or no, a score) on the repeated decisions inside a job.

elements.name: Decision model
elements.what: A System One model: a situation and typed questions in, probabilities out, no text.
elements.open: No open model of this class; a general open model (GPT-OSS 120B) matched it on 60 test cases at about eight times the cost; a small classifier on your own cases (SetFit, GLiNER2)
elements.closed: Jev (TypeSafe AI), launched 15 September 2026
elements.pick: Jev at rung two, scored only on held-back cases
elements.why: 60 of 60 held-back cases set up per its docs, a third of a second, about $0.018 per 1,000 decisions; an embedding classifier beat it once labelled data existed, which is rung three.

components.name: Own models
components.what: Rung three: small models trained on the verified record, for less still.

elements.name: Own small models
elements.what: A small model trained on verified cases so it takes a decision for less.
elements.open: Open weights to start from: Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss
elements.closed: Closed models tuned by their makers, who keep the weights: OpenAI's tuned models cannot be downloaded, and its self-serve fine-tuning closed to new organisations on 7 May 2026
elements.pick: Later: a small Qwen or Gemma model trained on verified cases an open model or a person produced; one trained only on a customer's own cases belongs to that customer
elements.why: A step down must pass the holdout; the frontier model keeps the new cases. The customer owns what its own cases train and runs it on any compute, its own included, while the vendor's own small models train only on de-identified cases it has the right to keep. Adapters share one open base model, since serving is the cost that stays, and until a lawyer rules they learn from open models' answers and people's corrections, never a closed model's outputs: Anthropic's terms bar using its service to train competing models.

components.name: Perceiving
components.what: Reading documents, images and signals, and searching text at scale.

elements.name: Embeddings and reranking
elements.what: Turning text into vectors for search, and re-ordering results by relevance.
elements.open: Qwen3-Embedding and Microsoft harrier-oss lead the public retrieval leaderboard (MTEB); BGE rerankers
elements.closed: Gemini Embedding, Voyage (MongoDB), Cohere Rerank
elements.pick: Qwen3-Embedding, only once retrieval is measured as the bottleneck
elements.why: Open models lead the independent retrieval leaderboard and run anywhere, including where data must stay.

elements.name: Document reading
elements.what: Turning PDFs, scans and forms into structured text.
elements.open: markitdown (187,299 stars), Docling; MinerU is Apache 2.0 with extra terms that require a paid licence at large scale
elements.closed: Reducto, Azure Document Intelligence, Google Document AI, Mistral OCR
elements.pick: The frontier model reads the document; markitdown for bulk conversion
elements.why: Fewer moving parts until volume calls for a pipeline.

elements.name: Images and signals
elements.what: Understanding medical images and signals, such as ECG (electrocardiogram) traces and echo images, beside documents.
elements.open: MONAI for medical imaging (Apache 2.0, 253,000 downloads a week); NeuroKit2 and WFDB for ECG signals (both MIT). MedGemma is open weights under Google's Health AI Developer Foundations licence, not an open-source licence
elements.closed: FDA-cleared tools per task, such as Anumana's ECG-AI (cleared for low ejection fraction, and on 8 April 2026 for cardiac amyloidosis from a standard 12-lead ECG); of the 50 newest devices on the FDA's AI list, 39 are radiology and 3 cardiovascular
elements.pick: Read, never interpret: the agent reads the values the device already printed in its report and passes tracings and images to the clinician untouched; any interpretation needs FDA clearance, so it stays out of a booking job
elements.why: Booking a test needs the order and the report, not a reading of the trace. Software that analyses a medical image or signal is regulated as a device, outside the exemption for decision support (Trust: Rules of the vertical).

components.name: Speaking and listening
components.what: Voice in and out, for phone calls and voice surfaces.

elements.name: Speech to text
elements.what: Transcribing calls and voice notes.
elements.open: Mistral Voxtral Small (2.8% word errors); Whisper, the most used
elements.closed: Microsoft MAI-Transcribe-2 (2.0% word errors, $1.67 per 1,000 minutes; in preview in Azure Speech), ElevenLabs Scribe v2 (2.2%, $3.67), Deepgram Nova-3 (5.2%)
elements.pick: MAI-Transcribe-2 where accuracy matters most, once it leaves preview and, with health data, Microsoft's business associate agreement covers it; Scribe v2 until then; the live-call model chosen on delay measured on the entity's own calls
elements.why: It is the most accurate and under half the price of Scribe v2. The speed figures are batch runs, not the delay on a live call, so live calls are measured, not assumed.

elements.name: Text to speech
elements.what: A natural voice for calls.
elements.open: Chatterbox (MIT), Kokoro (Apache 2.0; no change since 6 August 2025). Fish Speech is research and non-commercial use only, so not open source
elements.closed: Cartesia Sonic 3.6 (first on the voice arena, score 1277) and Google Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS (1268, within the margin, at $16.5 per million characters against Cartesia's $49); ElevenLabs' best model is twelfth
elements.pick: Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS or Cartesia, whichever answers faster on the entity's own test calls
elements.why: The two are tied on quality and Gemini costs a third as much; on a phone call, the delay before the first word decides. ElevenLabs is the runner-up and the most adopted (2.1 million Python downloads a week, every agent route), but its best model ranks twelfth on the voice arena and costs $50 per million characters, against Gemini's $16.50. Cartesia is the easier of the two picks for an agent to drive (a hosted MCP server, a CLI and skills), so the test call decides between them.

elements.name: Realtime voice
elements.what: Spoken conversation with low delay, end to end.
elements.closed: OpenAI Realtime, Gemini Live; Vapi and Retell for phone agents
elements.pick: LiveKit Agents on a Telnyx SIP trunk (a line for phone calls over the internet) to the agent's own number (LiveKit's own US number for a first test)
elements.why: It is the most used of the two open options (869,585 PyPI plus 779,499 npm downloads a week, against Pipecat's 237,232) and keeps speech, model and voice swappable on the agent's own number. LiveKit documents Telnyx trunks step by step. ElevenLabs Agents is the runner-up; Vapi is the quickest managed path at $0.05 a minute.

components.name: Making media
components.what: Images and video for content, ads and product.

elements.name: Image generation
elements.what: Pictures for content, ads and product.
elements.open: ComfyUI with open weights (Ideogram 4.0 open, Qwen-Image)
elements.closed: OpenAI gpt-image-2.5 (first on the image arena)
elements.pick: gpt-image-2.5 through the gateway, paid per use
elements.why: For content and ads only; the best open-weights model is eighth on the image arena (27 September 2026).

elements.name: Video generation
elements.what: Short video for content and ads.
elements.open: MiniMax H3 (the best open weights, eighth), Wan 2.2
elements.closed: Google Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash (first on the video arena)
elements.pick: Gemini Omni through the gateway, paid per use
elements.why: Buy per clip for content and ads; nothing to host.

components.name: Routing
components.what: The right model for each piece of work, through one gateway.

elements.name: Model gateway
elements.what: One API to many models, with fallbacks.
elements.closed: OpenRouter (Stripe agreed to buy it, August 2026), Vercel AI Gateway
elements.pick: Vercel AI Gateway
elements.why: It carries Jev and open models; a gateway owned by a payments company is a concentration risk, and a retired model is swapped here by configuration and re-verified. Agents that serve customers get metered access through it. OpenRouter is the runner-up and the more agent-native (a hosted MCP server, a CLI, 19 skills, per-agent keys by API) and the most used (8 million users, 100 trillion tokens a month), but it charges 5.5% on credit and Stripe has agreed to buy it; Vercel charges no markup or platform fee, even when the entity brings its own keys.

elements.name: Routing rule
elements.what: Judgement on the flagship, bulk work on cheaper models, repeated decisions down the ladder once a holdout proves it.
elements.closed: Not Diamond, Martian, Jev Router
elements.pick: The entity's own rule: route by task
elements.why: Maximum intelligence per task per token; every step down gated by a holdout.

categories.name: Harness
categories.question: What is it made of?
categories.what: The eleven components that turn a model into an agent.

components.name: Identity
components.what: The self: who it is at work, its job and its grade. Its addresses and proof live under Reach; its standing under Money and Company.

elements.name: Character and boundaries
elements.what: Personality, tone and what it will never do.
elements.closed: Persona settings inside hosted agents (custom GPTs, Copilot Autopilot)
elements.pick: SOUL.md
elements.why: Plain files anyone can read and diff.

elements.name: Operating instructions
elements.what: How it works in this job and codebase.
elements.closed: Vendor instruction fields (custom GPT instructions)
elements.pick: AGENTS.md plus CLAUDE.md and Claude Code's rule files
elements.why: AGENTS.md is the cross-runtime standard, in the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation since 9 December 2025; CLAUDE.md points at it.

elements.name: Name and brand
elements.what: A one-word symbolic name and a tagline; its look comes from the company's brand (Growth).
elements.closed: Brand kits in Figma or Canva
elements.pick: BRAND.md in the agent's own folder: one symbolic word and a tagline
elements.why: Every agent gets its own brand on one design system.

elements.name: Contract and definition of done
elements.what: The job, what counts as done and how it is verified, signed with the people who do the work today.
elements.open: A CONTRACT.md file with seven fields (name, owns, receives, produces, can decide, escalates, done means)
elements.closed: None worth naming: each hosted platform keeps its own job settings
elements.pick: One-page contract per agent
elements.why: If the work cannot be verified, the agent is not built.

elements.name: Grade
elements.what: Its salary band, which also caps the compute it may spend.
elements.closed: None worth naming
elements.pick: The grade sets the number: the salary band, and the compute and spending caps that follow from it
elements.why: An uncapped agent on the frontier model can cost about $2,000 a month.

elements.name: Owner of record
elements.what: The person it reports to, shown on the org chart where one exists.
elements.open: A field kept with the agent
elements.closed: The manager field in the customer's directory (Microsoft Entra, Okta)
elements.pick: A named owner on each agent, the person it reports to
elements.why: Every entity needs a named person who answers for it; proving who the agent is lives under Reach: Proof.

components.name: Memory
components.what: What it keeps between runs, for itself and for each person it serves.

elements.name: Working context
elements.what: What is in front of the model now: loading, compaction and handoff.
elements.open: SoL-Pi (NVIDIA) for pruning what is sent
elements.closed: Compaction built into Claude Code, Codex and the OpenAI Agents API
elements.pick: The runtime's compaction plus a handoff file, measured as tokens saved per run
elements.why: SoL-Pi cut token traffic by 45 to 49 percent at similar accuracy in September 2026.

elements.name: Long-term memory
elements.what: Facts, preferences and history that survive between sessions.
elements.closed: Supermemory cloud, Zep, Mem0 Platform
elements.pick: Plain files first, then Mem0's hosted memory when an agent needs a shared store; Supermemory as the close runner-up
elements.why: Every memory benchmark is run by a vendor, and Letta found a plain filesystem agent competitive, so files come first; Graphiti when facts change over time. For the hosted layer Mem0 now leads on use, about four times Supermemory's weekly downloads (620,090 against 149,990) and twice the stars, and its agent can start before any person signs up; both have a hosted MCP server, a CLI and skills and both start free.

elements.name: Shared knowledge
elements.what: The company brain: documents and notes every agent reads.
elements.open: Markdown in git, Microsoft GraphRAG. Obsidian, the editor, is closed source
elements.closed: Glean, Notion AI
elements.pick: A wiki engine over Markdown
elements.why: The Markdown stays the source of truth, and every brain also reads as a website.

elements.name: Rules from corrections
elements.what: Every correction a person made, kept as rules the next run obeys.
elements.closed: None worth naming
elements.pick: LEARNINGS.md and rule files
elements.why: A correction that vanishes trains the expert to stop correcting.

components.name: Skills
components.what: Packaged know-how it loads when a task needs it.

elements.name: Skill files
elements.what: Instructions, scripts and examples per task, loaded on demand (SKILL.md).
elements.closed: Skill stores inside Claude and ChatGPT
elements.pick: SKILL.md
elements.why: One open format read by 46 agent clients (agentskills.io, read 27 September 2026), including Codex, Copilot, Gemini CLI and Cursor.

elements.name: Skill library
elements.what: Where skills are found, shared and ranked.
elements.open: superpowers (292,160 stars, the most-starred), ECC, anthropics/skills
elements.closed: ClawHub, and the skill directories inside Claude and ChatGPT
elements.pick: superpowers as the base; rank the rest with a registry that scores skills by evidence
elements.why: The most-starred skills library, with a strong public record.

components.name: Tools
components.what: What it can call: command-line tools, the web, a computer.

elements.name: Command-line tools
elements.what: Deterministic programs for repeatable actions.
elements.closed: None worth naming: the leading command-line tools are open
elements.pick: playwright-cli and gh
elements.why: Connect in this order: an MCP server or a CLI, then a connector, then the API, and the screen last. Both picks are widely used, with a strong public record.

elements.name: Browser use
elements.what: Driving a browser: opening pages, clicking, typing and reading them.
elements.closed: Claude in Chrome, ChatGPT agent mode
elements.pick: Stagehand for each agent; playwright-cli for the operator's own work
elements.why: Stagehand v4 is built for agents and runs on the hosted browser; browser-use leads on stars (116,499).

elements.name: Computer use
elements.what: Operating a desktop and its apps by looking at the screen.
elements.closed: Claude computer use, OpenAI's computer-using agent
elements.pick: The default Claude model's computer use
elements.why: Claude Opus 5 leads OSWorld 2.0 (44.3%), the harder test; the older OSWorld-Verified board is near saturation and led by other models. Cua is the open fallback.

elements.name: Web search and extraction
elements.what: Finding and reading pages, with typed records where they exist.
elements.open: Firecrawl (AGPL-3.0, 185,489 stars, can run on your own machines), Crawl4AI (84,353), SearXNG (37,684)
elements.closed: Firecrawl's hosted service, Exa, Tavily
elements.pick: Firecrawl with its Alexandria providers
elements.why: It is the most-starred open option, runs self-hosted or hosted, and its Alexandria providers return typed records where they exist.

components.name: Hooks
components.what: Automation that fires at fixed points in its work.

elements.name: Lifecycle hooks
elements.what: Before and after a session, a tool call or a compaction.
elements.closed: The host runtime's own hooks (Claude Code is the reference)
elements.pick: plannotator
elements.why: A widely used hooks project with a strong public record; a hook is where a rule stops being a request.

elements.name: Policy hooks
elements.what: Checks that block an action before it runs.
elements.open: Open Policy Agent; hooks in the host runtime
elements.closed: None worth naming
elements.pick: The rules from Trust: Controls, as data, enforced by one engine before each tool call
elements.why: A rule blocks only when false alarms are near zero, and every override writes a ledger row.

components.name: Sub-agents
components.what: Fresh-context helpers it delegates to.

elements.name: Personas
elements.what: Packaged helpers with a narrow scope.
elements.closed: Claude Code sub-agents and teams, OpenAI Agents API sub-agents
elements.pick: wshobson/agents
elements.why: Few sub-agent listings carry scored evidence yet, so this pick is judgement, not a ranking.

elements.name: Parallel swarm
elements.what: Many helpers at once, briefed and verified by a lead.
elements.closed: Claude Code agent teams, OpenAI Agents API
elements.pick: Claude Code sub-agents; how many run at once is set by the machine's free memory
elements.why: Sub-agents come with the agent loop, and free memory, not a fixed count, limits how many run at once.

components.name: MCPs
components.what: Servers it connects to over the Model Context Protocol.

elements.name: Connected servers
elements.what: Real servers for the systems it uses; keys held outside the agent.
elements.open: github-mcp and the open server ecosystem
elements.closed: Vendor-hosted remote servers (Stripe, Supabase, GitHub)
elements.pick: github-mcp first; each agent gets its own address and tools on its product's MCP server (Surfaces: For agents)
elements.why: The server most coding agents need first; build to the 28 July 2026 version of the standard, which keeps nothing between calls.

elements.name: Server registry
elements.what: Where servers are found and vetted.
elements.closed: Smithery (Arcade bought it in August 2026)
elements.pick: Vet servers with a registry that ranks them by evidence; listing the entity's own is under Network: Discovery
elements.why: A listing is not proof a server works: about half of the listed servers complete a handshake.

components.name: Dispatch
components.what: Who does what, and when work fires on its own.

elements.name: Agent loop
elements.what: The runtime that reads the files, calls the model and runs the tools.
elements.open: OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, OpenCode, Codex CLI
elements.closed: Claude Code, Claude Managed Agents, OpenAI Agents API
elements.pick: The Claude Agent SDK is the loop (Claude Code for the operator's own work); Managed Agents hosts it for customers who have an API account
elements.why: One loop serves the operator's own work and every agent; OpenCode is the free worker for checks in a sandbox.

elements.name: Work routing
elements.what: Sending each task to the right agent and skill.
elements.closed: Claude Managed Agents, OpenAI Agents API
elements.pick: The Claude Agent SDK; LangGraph or Mastra where fixed steps with approval points are needed
elements.why: PocketFlow has had no push since 26 July 2026. LangGraph offers agents more ways in (a hosted docs server, a CLI and skills), but each agent already runs the Agent SDK's loop, so a second framework comes in only where fixed steps with approval points need a graph.

elements.name: Schedules
elements.what: Heartbeats and routine runs (HEARTBEAT.md, cron).
elements.closed: Claude Code routines, Inngest
elements.pick: HEARTBEAT.md, started by the host's scheduler; long runs go to durable execution (Operations: Runtime)
elements.why: One heartbeat per agent; anything that must survive a crash runs as a durable task.

elements.name: Event triggers
elements.what: Work that starts when something happens in a connected system, such as a new referral or a cancelled slot, instead of polling for it.
elements.open: Activepieces (MIT outside its enterprise folder, 24,753 stars); CloudEvents, the CNCF's standard event format. n8n (206,125 stars) is fair-code under its Sustainable Use License, not open source
elements.closed: Composio's triggers (hosted; its SDK is MIT, 1.1 million npm downloads a week); Zapier; Pipedream (Workday agreed to buy it on 19 November 2025; over 3,000 apps)
elements.pick: Composio's triggers for apps connected through it, and the records system's own event feeds where they exist; each event lands in a durable queue (Operations: Durable execution) that wakes the right agent; polling only where no event exists
elements.why: Polling spends model calls on nothing and notices late; a trigger wakes the agent only when there is work.

components.name: Evals
components.what: Proof that it works and that a change helped.

elements.name: Golden tasks and judges
elements.what: Cases with known right answers, graded pass or fail.
elements.closed: Braintrust, LangSmith
elements.pick: promptfoo in continuous integration (the checks that run on every change), pinned to a version, with Inspect as the neutral judge
elements.why: OpenAI announced on 9 March 2026 that it would buy promptfoo and keep it open source; it is still MIT and active (807,194 npm downloads a week). Inspect, from the UK AI Security Institute, is a judge no lab owns.

elements.name: Held-back cases
elements.what: Cases nobody tuned on; the only ones that count.
elements.closed: Vendor graders (Managed Agents Outcomes)
elements.pick: About 200 per decision
elements.why: Sixty cases cannot tell 97% from 99%.

elements.name: Public benchmarks
elements.what: Shared tests that compare models and harnesses on someone else's job.
elements.closed: Artificial Analysis and Arena, the hosted leaderboards
elements.pick: Read them to shortlist; decide on the entity's own held-back cases
elements.why: A benchmark measures someone else's job, never the entity's own.

elements.name: Simulated environments
elements.what: Clones of the buyer's systems and simulated users, for trying work that cannot be tried live first.
elements.open: tau-bench's simulated users, OSWorld, Prime Intellect's environments
elements.closed: Private environment vendors
elements.pick: Held-back cases first; a simulated clone once live trials are too risky
elements.why: Some jobs cannot be practised on real patients or real money.

elements.name: Test suite
elements.what: Unit, integration and end-to-end tests that gate every change.
elements.closed: None worth naming: the leading test tools are open
elements.pick: Vitest and Playwright
elements.why: A change ships only when the suite passes.

elements.name: Fairness and bias tests
elements.what: Verifying that outcomes do not differ unfairly across groups wherever the job decides about people, such as who is offered the earliest slot.
elements.open: Fairlearn (MIT, 27,000 downloads a week) for group metrics; AIF360 (Apache 2.0); deepeval's bias metric (Apache 2.0)
elements.closed: Governance suites with bias monitoring: IBM watsonx.governance, Fiddler
elements.pick: Before any agent ranks or prioritises people, such as patients: compare outcomes on the held-back cases (waiting time, slot offered, calls made) across the groups the law protects where the data allows, plus language and insurer, with Fairlearn's metrics, before launch and after every change the loop ships; the agent never sees a protected trait its job does not need
elements.why: The framework of NIST (the US standards institute) asks for fairness to be evaluated and documented (MEASURE 2.11). Since 1 May 2025, US health programs that take federal money must not discriminate through patient care decision support tools (45 CFR 92.210), so an agent that ranks patients for care needs this verification.

components.name: Observability
components.what: What each run did, what it cost and what value it made.

elements.name: Traces
elements.what: Every step of every run, replayable.
elements.closed: LangSmith, Datadog LLM Observability
elements.pick: Langfuse
elements.why: ClickHouse has owned Langfuse since January 2026 and the core is still MIT; write traces in the open OpenTelemetry format so the tool can be changed.

elements.name: Cost and value receipts
elements.what: Cost per run beside value per token and the share a person signed off; the totals per agent are defined under Money: Books.
elements.closed: None worth naming
elements.pick: A home-made receipt per run
elements.why: Compute spent on unverified work shows as waste, not cost of goods.

components.name: Sandbox
components.what: The sealed place where its code runs.

elements.name: Isolated runs
elements.what: A fresh machine per run for untrusted code.
elements.open: E2B's own runtime (Apache 2.0; it runs in E2B's cloud or on your own machines), OpenSandbox (15,532 stars), microsandbox (8,447)
elements.closed: E2B, Modal, Cloudflare Sandboxes
elements.pick: E2B
elements.why: It gives each run a small sealed virtual machine (Firecracker) that started in 1.6 seconds at the median in a published test (E2B says about 150 ms). It is also the open leader by use: 2.14 million npm and 1.32 million PyPI downloads a week. Daytona's core went private in June 2026. Vercel Sandbox is the runner-up: the most downloaded sandbox SDK (5.83 million a week), a CLI and a skill, and microVMs on a Vercel account, though the CLI and skill are the Vercel platform's, not the sandbox's own. E2B's only hosted MCP server is its docs server, since its control server's repository was archived, so agents drive it through its SDK or CLI.

elements.name: Network and file limits
elements.what: What a run may reach, keep and send out.
elements.open: A gate that lets a run reach only listed addresses (Envoy, Squid)
elements.closed: Network controls in E2B and Modal
elements.pick: Deny by default, with an allow-list per agent
elements.why: What a run cannot reach, it cannot leak.

categories.name: Reach
categories.question: How does it reach the world and act in it as itself?
categories.what: Its own addresses, the workstation it acts through, and the proof of who it is. Own the self; rent the addresses.

components.name: Addresses
components.what: Where people and agents reach it as itself.

elements.name: Email inbox
elements.what: Its own mailbox, readable by the agent.
elements.closed: AgentMail
elements.pick: AgentMail
elements.why: An agent can do the whole job itself: AgentMail has a hosted MCP server in the official registry, a CLI, skills and an API, and creates an inbox in one call with no domain, which no long-standing mailbox offers; it is backed by Y Combinator and downloaded over 500,000 times a week. Google Workspace, the runner-up, fits when a customer wants the mailbox inside its own tenant. The free plan allows 3 inboxes; the $20 Developer plan allows 10.

elements.name: Phone number, calls and SMS
elements.what: Its own number, inbound and outbound.
elements.closed: Telnyx, Twilio, Plivo
elements.pick: Telnyx: the agent's own number for calls and texts, bought and wired by the agent itself
elements.why: US carriers require business text numbers to be registered first (10DLC). Telnyx is the only carrier where an agent can do the whole job itself: a hosted MCP server that calls the real API (Twilio's official one only searches its docs), official skills, a CLI that buys and wires a number in one command, and a published agent sign-up; a US number costs $1.00 a month and a text from $0.004, against Twilio's $1.15 and $0.0083. Twilio is the runner-up: its software is downloaded about 18 times as often.

elements.name: WhatsApp
elements.what: Its own WhatsApp Business number.
elements.open: Only unofficial libraries (whatsapp-web.js, Baileys), which break WhatsApp's terms
elements.closed: Meta's WhatsApp Business Platform, directly or through Telnyx, Kapso or Twilio
elements.pick: WhatsApp on the agent's own Telnyx number, the same account as its calls and texts; Kapso if Meta's sign-up through Telnyx stalls
elements.why: Meta barred general-purpose assistants in January 2026 and readmitted them for a fee in March; on 9 June 2026 the European Commission ordered free access for rival AI assistants while its case runs. A business's own service agent was never the target. One number and one account for calls, texts and WhatsApp, under the same hosted MCP server, CLI and skills; Kapso is the most agent-native WhatsApp layer and the fallback.

elements.name: iMessage
elements.what: Blue bubbles, reachable from any iPhone.
elements.open: BlueBubbles, Photon's imessage-kit (both need a Mac)
elements.closed: Sendblue, Linq, Blooio (hosted lines); Apple Messages for Business, the only route Apple sanctions
elements.pick: Sendblue for the agent's own line; apply to Apple Messages for Business; Photon only for the owner's own handle
elements.why: Hosted dedicated lines exist, so the agent's own line can run in the cloud rather than on a Mac.

elements.name: Slack, Teams, Discord and Telegram
elements.what: Its identity inside the chat apps where teams already work.
elements.open: Vercel Chat SDK (15 channel adapters), grammY, discord.js, Slack Bolt
elements.closed: Each platform's own bot identity: a Slack app, a Teams app in the customer's Entra, a Discord or Telegram bot
elements.pick: One app or bot per agent on each platform, through the Chat SDK adapters under one identity layer
elements.why: Fifteen maintained adapters, instead of writing and maintaining one per platform.

elements.name: Social media handles
elements.what: Its own accounts on X, LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube.
elements.closed: The official APIs: X (paid per use since February 2026), Instagram, TikTok, YouTube
elements.pick: Company-owned accounts only, each labelled as automated, with a person approving each post; never a person's account. The posting tool is decided once, under Growth: Content (Postiz)
elements.why: X requires an automated label and LinkedIn forbids automating a member's account; nothing is posted in public without a yes.

elements.name: Domain and web address
elements.what: Its own name on the web and on email.
elements.closed: Cloudflare Registrar
elements.pick: Cloudflare
elements.why: Sold at cost; it also holds the email settings (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) that keep its mail out of spam.

elements.name: Calendar
elements.what: Time others can book with it.
elements.closed: Google and Microsoft 365 calendars; Cal.com hosted
elements.pick: Its own Google or Microsoft 365 calendar where the customer works; hosted Cal.com for public booking links
elements.why: Meetings get booked where the customer already lives.

elements.name: Meetings
elements.what: Joining calls as itself, to listen, take notes or speak.
elements.closed: Recall.ai
elements.pick: Recall.ai, when a job needs meetings
elements.why: A meeting is a door people use. Recall.ai is the most adopted meeting-bot API ($0.50 an hour of recording, the first 5 hours free); its hosted MCP server reads bots and workspace data, while sending a bot into a call still goes through its API, through a small custom tool. Vexa is the open runner-up.

elements.name: Postal address
elements.what: Where mail, cheques and deliveries arrive, scanned for the agent.
elements.open: None: an address needs a building and people to handle the mail
elements.closed: Stable (an API for scanned mail and cheque images); LegalZoom Virtual Mail, formerly Earth Class Mail (1.7 million cheques deposited); PostScan Mail (developer API)
elements.pick: Stable: one address per company, not per agent; the agent reads scans through the API with a key the secrets keeper holds, and the service deposits cheques into the bank; LegalZoom Virtual Mail as the swap
elements.why: Every mailbox service needs US Postal Service Form 1583, signed by a named person who shows photo ID, so the address runs through a person like the tax number; Stable's published examples feed scanned mail to a model (updated April 2026).

elements.name: Fax
elements.what: Sending and receiving faxes, which payers and practices still use, for example for prior authorisations.
elements.closed: Telnyx Programmable Fax, on the same account as calls and texts
elements.pick: Telnyx Programmable Fax on a fax-enabled number, when a vertical still runs on fax, such as prior authorisations in health care
elements.why: Payers still take prior authorisation packets by fax; Telnyx buys a fax-enabled number and sends a fax by API on the same account as calls and texts. With health data, first confirm that Telnyx will sign a HIPAA (the US health privacy law) business associate agreement for fax.

components.name: Workstation
components.what: What it acts through: a computer, a browser and connectors to other apps.

elements.name: Cloud desktop
elements.what: A desktop of its own in the cloud, kept between tasks; computer use under Harness drives it.
elements.closed: Orgo (from $29 a computer a month), Windows 365 for Agents
elements.pick: Orgo; Windows 365 for Agents when the customer runs Microsoft
elements.why: Orgo publishes its price, from $29 a computer a month; Cua is the open fallback.

elements.name: Signed-in browser
elements.what: A browser of its own that stays signed in and outlives any one machine; the browser tool under Harness drives it.
elements.open: Steel Browser (self-hosted); Browserless (SSPL, not open source)
elements.closed: Browserbase, Kernel
elements.pick: Browserbase
elements.why: Stagehand runs on it, its sessions stay signed in between tasks, and 10,000 companies use it.

elements.name: Code account
elements.what: Its own account on the code host, so its commits and reviews carry its name.
elements.closed: A GitHub App or machine account
elements.pick: A GitHub App per agent
elements.why: Scoped, revocable, and never a person's seat.

elements.name: App connectors
elements.what: Reaching every other app with the owner's grant, never its password, and never with more access than the person it works for.
elements.closed: Composio, Nango, Pipedream Connect (Workday's; its code is source-available), Arcade
elements.pick: Composio
elements.why: The most downloaded of the four agent-connector SDKs, and the agent never holds the app's key; the owner consents once per app.

elements.name: Files and storage
elements.what: Its own drive for documents it makes and receives.
elements.closed: Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive, Dropbox
elements.pick: The customer's own drive through a connector; its own copies in the storage under Software: Data stores
elements.why: Files live where the customer already works.

elements.name: Private network access
elements.what: Reaching systems behind a buyer's firewall through an outbound tunnel or a private link, never an opening in the firewall.
elements.open: frp (Apache 2.0, 109,653 stars); Headscale (BSD 3-Clause, 44,168), an open control server for Tailscale's clients; cloudflared, Cloudflare's connector (Apache 2.0, 15,936)
elements.closed: Cloudflare Tunnel, Tailscale, ngrok; AWS PrivateLink and Google Private Service Connect inside one cloud
elements.pick: MCP tunnels: the buyer runs an outbound-only cloudflared connector next to a private MCP server with its own sign-in per server, so no inbound port opens and the agent never holds the credentials; for a health system, its own integration engine or a site-to-site VPN (virtual private network) when its security team requires one
elements.why: Hospitals keep their systems behind firewalls, and their security review decides the route. An outbound-only tunnel opens no inbound port, so the firewall stays shut.

components.name: Proof
components.what: How anyone knows it is this agent, acting for this person.

elements.name: Verifiable agent identity
elements.what: An identity others can verify, tied to its owner.
elements.open: SPIFFE; auth.md (WorkOS); MCP client metadata documents
elements.closed: Microsoft Entra Agent ID; Visa and Mastercard agent key registries
elements.pick: Each agent its own OAuth client and signing key; Entra Agent ID for Microsoft customers
elements.why: Card networks now verify agents by signature, and Microsoft made the agent a directory object.

elements.name: Signed requests to websites
elements.what: Proving to a website that a request comes from a known agent.
elements.open: Web Bot Auth (HTTP Message Signatures; an IETF working group)
elements.closed: Cloudflare signed agents, Visa Trusted Agent Protocol, Mastercard Agent Pay
elements.pick: Sign every outbound request with the agent's own key
elements.why: Websites and card networks tell known agents from bots this way.

elements.name: Know your agent
elements.what: Proving to merchants and card networks which person or company stands behind it; who may call its own doors is under Trust: Controls (Callers it lets in).
elements.open: KYAPay (Skyfire), AP2 (Google's Agent Payments Protocol) mandates
elements.closed: Visa Intelligent Commerce, Mastercard agentic tokens; Persona, Trulioo
elements.pick: Whatever the card issuer requires: Visa Intelligent Commerce tokens, through Ramp
elements.why: Merchants and card networks now ask who stands behind an agent.

elements.name: Scoped credentials
elements.what: The keys and tokens that prove this agent, one set each, scoped to its job.
elements.closed: Issued by each service it signs in to
elements.pick: One key set per agent, scoped to its job and held by the secrets keeper under Trust: Security, never by the agent
elements.why: Reach lists what the keys prove; where they are kept is decided once, under Trust.

elements.name: Mandate
elements.what: A signed statement of what it may commit its owner to (spend, sign, accept terms), with limits and an expiry, that others can verify.
elements.open: AP2's mandates (Apache 2.0): an open mandate holds the limits, a closed mandate binds one act, and the owner approves on a screen the agent cannot touch; the specification work moved to the FIDO Alliance in 2026
elements.closed: Visa Intelligent Commerce and Mastercard Agent Pay (both launched April 2025; both joined AP2 in September 2025); AWS AgentCore Payments' spending limits
elements.pick: A mandate per agent beside its contract and permissions file: what it may buy and up to how much, that it may not sign or accept terms unless the owner adds it, and an expiry; the owner signs it and the tool layer verifies it before each act; AP2's format when a payment network asks for one
elements.why: Scoped keys prove who is acting; a mandate proves what the owner agreed to, which is what a merchant, a card network or a court will ask for. If each agent has a permissions file and a hard spending cap, the mandate is their signed, portable form.

categories.name: Surfaces
categories.question: How do people and other agents use it?
categories.what: The doors: first-party places people go, and interfaces other agents call. Messaging channels are Reach, not surfaces.

components.name: For people
components.what: Places a person goes to use it.

elements.name: Front door
elements.what: One presence behind every door; a manager agent routes each job and follows it to the finish. Its number and address are under Reach.
elements.open: OpenClaw (one gateway, many channels), Vercel Chat SDK
elements.closed: Sierra (customer-facing agents across channels)
elements.pick: The entity: one presence behind every door, named by its person
elements.why: One memory, and the person never has to know which agent to ask.

elements.name: Web app
elements.what: The main place to hire, watch and approve its work.
elements.closed: No closed framework leads; builders such as Lovable and v0
elements.pick: A web app on the framework under Software: Front end (Next.js)
elements.why: React is used by 44.7% and Next.js by 20.8% of developers (Stack Overflow 2025 survey), and the rest of the stack assumes it.

elements.name: Mobile app
elements.what: iOS and Android, with push notifications.
elements.closed: Native Swift and Kotlin
elements.pick: An Expo app, on the mobile framework under Software: Front end
elements.why: One codebase for both stores.

elements.name: Desktop app
elements.what: A native app when a job needs local files or always-on presence.
elements.closed: None: native toolkits
elements.pick: Electron; Tauri when install size matters
elements.why: Electron is the leader by use. Tauri has more agent doors (an llms.txt among them) and smaller installs, which is why it takes over when install size matters.

elements.name: Browser extension
elements.what: Working inside the pages a person already uses.
elements.closed: None: the browser stores gate distribution
elements.pick: WXT
elements.why: Level with Plasmo on use, and not tied to one UI library.

elements.name: Embeddable widget
elements.what: A small window on someone else's site.
elements.closed: Intercom Messenger
elements.pick: assistant-ui
elements.why: About four times CopilotKit's weekly downloads.

elements.name: Inside other assistants
elements.what: An app that runs inside ChatGPT and Claude.
elements.open: MCP Apps (the first official MCP extension), mcp-use
elements.closed: ChatGPT's app directory, Claude's connectors directory
elements.pick: One MCP App, submitted to both directories
elements.why: One build, two stores; an MCP App is an MCP server with a screen, built on the server under For agents.

elements.name: Live view of its work
elements.what: Streaming what an agent is doing into a web app as it works.
elements.open: AG-UI, the Agent-User Interaction protocol (2.41 million downloads a week)
elements.closed: None found
elements.pick: AG-UI when an agent streams its work into the entity's own app
elements.why: The standard way to show an agent working, so the viewer can step in.

elements.name: Editor extensions
elements.what: Working inside the code editors builders already use.
elements.open: The Agent Client Protocol (ACP, Apache 2.0), started by Zed, with official SDKs in five languages; its TypeScript SDK has 7.4 million npm downloads a week. Zed itself is GPL 3.0 (90,967 stars)
elements.closed: Cursor (SpaceX closed its $60 billion purchase on 14 August 2026), GitHub Copilot in VS Code, JetBrains AI
elements.pick: Later: one ACP adapter so a builder can call an agent from any editor that speaks it; a VS Code extension only if builders ask
elements.why: Wait until builders are customers; then one protocol reaches every editor that adopts it, where an extension reaches one.

components.name: For agents
components.what: Interfaces other agents and programs call.

elements.name: API
elements.what: A plain HTTP API with typed inputs and outputs.
elements.closed: API gateways (Kong, Apigee)
elements.pick: Hono with Zod and an OpenAPI file; Scalar for the reference page
elements.why: Agents read OpenAPI, and the SDK and MCP server can be generated from it.

elements.name: Its MCP server
elements.what: Its tools offered to any assistant.
elements.open: The official TypeScript SDK; FastMCP for Python
elements.closed: Hosting on Cloudflare Workers or Vercel; listing on Smithery
elements.pick: One hosted MCP server per product, built with the official SDK through mcp-handler on Vercel, with an address and tools of its own for each entity (a path per entity) and its own scoped keys
elements.why: The official SDK leads by far (63.7 million downloads a week); where it is listed is decided under Network: Discovery. A door belongs to the lowest layer that uses it: one deployment per product serves hundreds of entities, while each entity keeps its own address, tools and keys.

elements.name: CLI
elements.what: An installable command for builders and agents.
elements.closed: None: shipped through npm and Homebrew
elements.pick: npm package with a bin
elements.why: commander leads by far.

elements.name: Agent card
elements.what: A public description other agents read before hiring it (/.well-known/agent-card.json since A2A 1.0).
elements.closed: Hosted agent cards in Google Agent Engine and Microsoft Foundry
elements.pick: A2A card on every agent
elements.why: So any assistant can hire it.

elements.name: Agent sign-up
elements.what: Letting another agent sign itself up and get its own key, without a person.
elements.closed: Firecrawl's agent sign-up, Stripe Projects
elements.pick: The auth.md pattern on the entity's own API
elements.why: An onboarding an agent can finish sells to every agent that reads it.

elements.name: SDKs
elements.what: Client libraries in the languages builders use.
elements.closed: Stainless, Speakeasy
elements.pick: Hey API for a TypeScript client from the API's OpenAPI file
elements.why: Buy a generator only when shipping several languages.

elements.name: Plugins and skill packages
elements.what: Its skills, hooks and server bundled for other harnesses.
elements.closed: ChatGPT's app directory, Claude's connectors directory
elements.pick: Skills as SKILL.md inside a Claude Code plugin
elements.why: The same skills work in any tool that reads the open format.

elements.name: Webhooks and events
elements.what: Telling other systems when work is done.
elements.open: Svix (MIT; the Standard Webhooks scheme), Hookdeck Outpost (Apache 2.0). Convoy ships under its own licence
elements.closed: Svix Cloud, Hookdeck
elements.pick: Svix
elements.why: One signing scheme, so one verifier covers many platforms.

components.name: Docs
components.what: How people and agents learn to use it.

elements.name: Agent-readable docs
elements.what: llms.txt and a public AGENTS.md, so an agent calling it can read first.
elements.closed: Mintlify (generates llms.txt)
elements.pick: llms.txt, plus AGENTS.md in public repositories
elements.why: Cheap. Some coding tools and agents read them; no major assistant confirms reading llms.txt.

elements.name: Docs site
elements.what: Guides and reference for people.
elements.closed: Mintlify (20,000 companies)
elements.pick: Mintlify for each product's docs: its free Starter plan includes a custom domain and a hosted MCP server, and its sites publish llms.txt and a skills index for agents; Fumadocs where the docs must live inside the product's own app
elements.why: Other agents learn a product through its docs, and Mintlify gives them every door on its free plan; 20,000+ companies use it (its homepage). Fumadocs, the open runner-up, is built for Next.js and leads Docusaurus on weekly downloads, but gives agents only what the team builds itself.

components.name: Devices
components.what: Glasses, pendants, speakers and other bodies.

elements.name: Wearables and devices
elements.what: Reaching it without a screen.
elements.closed: Meta's glasses and pendant
elements.pick: Later: reach people through their phone channels first
elements.why: No build until a job needs hands-free.

categories.name: Software
categories.question: What are its doors built from?
categories.what: The building blocks behind the web and mobile surfaces. Adopt standard defaults here and keep each swappable.

components.name: Front end
components.what: What the person sees and touches.

elements.name: Framework
elements.what: The web framework.
elements.closed: No closed framework leads; builders such as Lovable and v0
elements.pick: Next.js
elements.why: The most used React framework (20.8% of developers, Stack Overflow 2025 survey), and the rest of the stack assumes it.

elements.name: UI kit and design system
elements.what: Components and design tokens.
elements.closed: Paid kits such as Tailwind Plus
elements.pick: shadcn/ui with shared design tokens
elements.why: Every surface gets the same colours and typeface.

elements.name: Accessibility
elements.what: Every surface usable with a keyboard and a screen reader and readable with low vision, measured against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG).
elements.open: WCAG 2.2 (a W3C standard); axe-core (MPL 2.0, 80.4 million npm downloads a week) and Pa11y (LGPL 3.0) to test
elements.closed: Deque's paid axe tools, Level Access, Siteimprove. Overlays do not make a site compliant: in 2025 the Federal Trade Commission ordered accessiBe to pay $1 million for claiming its AI widget could
elements.pick: WCAG 2.2 AA, which also meets the 2.1 AA that US rules cite, on every surface people use; axe-core inside Playwright tests on every change, plus a keyboard and screen-reader pass before each launch; never an overlay
elements.why: Health systems that take HHS funding must make their web content and mobile apps meet WCAG 2.1 AA by 11 May 2027 if they have 15 or more employees and by 10 May 2028 if smaller (HHS moved both dates on 7 May 2026), so a patient-facing booking page built for them must too. The European Accessibility Act has covered e-commerce and banking in the EU since June 2025.

elements.name: Mobile framework
elements.what: What the iOS and Android apps are built with.
elements.open: React Native (MIT, 126,749 stars, 15.1 million npm downloads a week) with Expo (MIT, 52,466 stars, 10.4 million a week); Flutter (BSD 3-Clause, 179,125 stars) leads on stars but is written in Dart
elements.closed: Apple's SwiftUI and Xcode for iOS-only apps (Kotlin and Jetpack Compose are open source but Android-only); Expo Application Services (EAS), Expo's hosted build service
elements.pick: Expo (React Native), with EAS for store builds and over-the-air updates; native Swift or Kotlin only for a feature Expo cannot reach
elements.why: One TypeScript codebase for both stores and the same React skills as the web app. TypeScript is used by 43.6 percent of developers and Dart by 5.9 percent (Stack Overflow survey, 2025), which is Flutter's cost for a TypeScript team.

components.name: Back end
components.what: Logic, APIs and the language it is written in.

elements.name: Runtime and language
elements.what: Where server code runs.
elements.closed: Edge runtimes inside the platforms (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Functions)
elements.pick: TypeScript on Node.js; Bun for command-line tools
elements.why: Node.js is used by 48.7% of developers (Stack Overflow 2025 survey).

components.name: Data stores
components.what: Where the product's data lives.

elements.name: Database
elements.what: The system of record.
elements.open: Supabase (110,814 stars), PocketBase, Appwrite; PostgreSQL underneath
elements.closed: Firebase (Google) among backend platforms; among databases alone, Oracle (first of 438 on DB-Engines, September 2026) and Microsoft SQL Server (30.1% of developers, the most used closed database); MongoDB Atlas
elements.pick: Supabase (Postgres)
elements.why: Supabase is the open-source leader among backend platforms built on Postgres: 110,814 GitHub stars, and its code library is downloaded 30.2 million times a week, 2.7 times Firebase's 11.1 million (npm, 20 to 26 September 2026); nearly 10 million developers build on it (June 2026). Among databases the open leader is PostgreSQL, which Supabase runs (55.6% of developers, Stack Overflow 2025 survey).

elements.name: Cache and limits on callers
elements.what: Fast shared storage and abuse limits, because each web request may run on a fresh server that remembers nothing.
elements.closed: Upstash Redis
elements.pick: Upstash Redis
elements.why: Nothing can be kept in a server's memory between requests on Vercel.

elements.name: Vector store
elements.what: Embeddings for product search.
elements.closed: Pinecone
elements.pick: pgvector inside Supabase for product search; memory's store follows Harness: Memory
elements.why: One database fewer.

elements.name: File storage and delivery
elements.what: Uploads, exports and assets, served fast (a CDN).
elements.closed: AWS S3, Cloudflare R2
elements.pick: Cloudflare R2
elements.why: No charge when files are downloaded.

elements.name: Search
elements.what: Search over the product's content.
elements.closed: Algolia
elements.pick: Postgres full-text search and pgvector first; Meilisearch when a separate engine is needed
elements.why: One database until search is the bottleneck.

components.name: Accounts and payments
components.what: Signing people in, and taking their money.

elements.name: Sign-in and user accounts
elements.what: Log-in, sessions, roles and single sign-on.
elements.open: Supabase Auth (MIT; it ships inside every Supabase install, 30.6 million downloads a week), Better Auth (MIT; the most downloaded stand-alone library, 10.35 million a week), Keycloak, Authentik
elements.closed: Clerk, Auth0 and Okta, WorkOS
elements.pick: Supabase Auth for products on a Supabase stack; Better Auth for a product that does not run on Supabase; WorkOS when an enterprise wants its own single sign-on and directory sync
elements.why: One system fewer: users stay in the product's Postgres, the database's row-level security (rules that keep each customer's rows apart) works with no token bridge, and its OAuth 2.1 server signs agents in over MCP. Better Auth would need a bridge to that security.

elements.name: Payment gateway
elements.what: Checkout, subscriptions and payouts.
elements.closed: Stripe
elements.pick: Stripe
elements.why: Businesses on Stripe processed $1.9 trillion in 2025, about 1.6% of world GDP (its annual letter). When the buyers are health systems, which pay invoices by bank transfer, card fees barely matter.

elements.name: Storefront for goods
elements.what: A catalogue, a cart and orders, for an entity that sells goods.
elements.open: Medusa (36,489 stars; MIT outside its enterprise files), Saleor (23,383; BSD-3-Clause)
elements.closed: Shopify, BigCommerce
elements.pick: Later, from the first goods sale: Shopify for a small shop; Medusa when the store's code and data must be the entity's own
elements.why: A store starts on Shopify in a day, and Shopify's API library gets 637,740 npm downloads a week against Medusa's 195,917; Medusa keeps the store the entity's own once goods become a real line of business.

components.name: Messaging
components.what: The product's own outbound email and notifications (not the agent's inbox).

elements.name: Transactional email
elements.what: Receipts, alerts and sign-in links.
elements.open: Nodemailer (the open library for sending mail, 25.8 million downloads a week), Postal, useSend; React Email for templates
elements.closed: Resend, Amazon SES, Postmark
elements.pick: Resend
elements.why: The most downloaded client for a hosted email service: 12.9 million a week, against SendGrid 5.3 million and Postmark 1.2 million.

elements.name: Push and in-app notifications
elements.what: Reaching people on phone and in the app.
elements.closed: Knock, OneSignal, Firebase Cloud Messaging
elements.pick: Expo push for the app; Novu when an inbox with preferences is needed
elements.why: Push rides on the mobile stack under Software: Front end.

components.name: Background jobs
components.what: Work that must not run inside a web request.

elements.name: Queues and schedules
elements.what: Retries, fan-out and scheduled work for the app.
elements.closed: Inngest, Trigger.dev
elements.pick: Trigger.dev, the engine under Operations: Durable execution
elements.why: One tool for the app's jobs and the agents' long runs; the choice and its reasons live in Operations.

components.name: Content and languages
components.what: Words and pages the team edits without code, in many languages.

elements.name: Content management
elements.what: Pages, posts and help articles edited without code.
elements.closed: Sanity
elements.pick: MDX files in the repo; Payload when non-engineers need an editor
elements.why: Agents and people edit the same files.

elements.name: Languages
elements.what: Translation and local formats.
elements.closed: Crowdin, Lokalise
elements.pick: next-intl
elements.why: i18next leads overall; next-intl fits the Next.js App Router.

categories.name: Network
categories.question: How does it work with other agents?
categories.what: The protocols it speaks, where others find it, the markets it is hired in, and the reputation it carries between them.

components.name: Protocols
components.what: The shared languages for tools, agents and payments.

elements.name: MCP (tools)
elements.what: How an agent connects to tools and data.
elements.closed: None: vendors adopted MCP
elements.pick: MCP, built to the version chosen under Harness: MCPs
elements.why: Every major lab and editor ships a client.

elements.name: A2A (agents)
elements.what: How agents hire and talk to other agents.
elements.closed: Hosted A2A in Google Agent Engine, Microsoft Foundry and AWS Bedrock AgentCore
elements.pick: A2A, through the card each agent publishes (Surfaces: For agents)
elements.why: Google proposed it on 9 April 2025 and 1.0 shipped on 12 March 2026; use it when another company's agent must hire this one, and treat every message as untrusted.

elements.name: Payments between agents
elements.what: How an agent pays or gets paid by another agent or a merchant.
elements.open: x402 (the Linux Foundation's x402 Foundation, announced 2 April 2026 and running since 14 July 2026), AP2
elements.closed: Stripe's agentic commerce suite (the Agentic Commerce Protocol, ACP, for ChatGPT); Google and Shopify's UCP (the Universal Commerce Protocol)
elements.pick: x402 for machine payments; ACP and UCP when selling through ChatGPT or Google
elements.why: All are live; x402's founding members include Coinbase, which gave the protocol, Stripe, Cloudflare and Amazon Web Services.

components.name: Discovery
components.what: Where other agents and people find it.

elements.name: Registries and directories
elements.what: Listings of agents and servers by what they do.
elements.open: The official MCP Registry, the AGNTCY Agent Directory
elements.closed: Microsoft Agent 365, Smithery (Arcade)
elements.pick: List each agent's server in the official registry; the agent card itself is under Surfaces
elements.why: Listings are where agents look first, but a listing is not proof a server works.

components.name: Markets
components.what: Where agents are hired and bought.

elements.name: Agent marketplaces
elements.what: Places where other agents hire an agent and pay per task.
elements.closed: Coinbase's Agentic.Market (x402 services, April 2026)
elements.pick: Later: list once other agents actually hire it
elements.why: No neutral market exists yet, and the record has to come first.

components.name: Hiring other agents
components.what: Contracts, budgets and verification when one agent hires another.

elements.name: Delegation contracts
elements.what: The job, the cap and the verification, agreed before another agent starts.
elements.closed: None worth naming
elements.pick: The job, the cap and the verification agreed before another agent starts, each hop with its own scoped grant
elements.why: Credentials leak across delegation hops in A2A as specified (A2ABreak, September 2026).

elements.name: Disputes and escrow
elements.what: Holding payment until another agent's work passes its verification, and settling a disagreement when it does not.
elements.open: ERC-8004's validation registry, where independent validators confirm work (a draft Ethereum standard, on mainnet since February 2026; its validation part is still being revised); escrow contracts built on OpenZeppelin (MIT, 27,254 stars)
elements.closed: Card holds: Stripe authorises a payment and captures it later, usually holding it for 7 days online; freelance marketplaces such as Upwork hold milestone payments and mediate disputes
elements.pick: Inside one company's own fleet, no escrow: the job, the cap and the verification are agreed first and nothing is paid until the verification passes. With another company's agent: authorise at hire, capture only after the verification, and a named person decides disputes; on-chain escrow only when a buyer pays in stablecoins
elements.why: Nobody offers a neutral referee between agents yet: a June 2026 study found ERC-8004's reputation records can be manipulated at little cost. Paying only after the verification is an escrow any company can run today.

components.name: Reputation
components.what: The record that travels with it between customers and markets.

elements.name: Portable record
elements.what: How the record travels: a public page and a signed export, with the owner's permission. The record itself is under Trust: Records.
elements.closed: None: no neutral reputation layer exists
elements.pick: A public record page and a signed export; with health data, counts, never cases
elements.why: Nobody offers one; a June 2026 study found ERC-8004's registry cannot yet serve as a trust signal.

categories.name: Physical world
categories.question: What does it make, keep, move or do off the screen, and through whom?
categories.what: Goods, stock, places, deliveries, and the hands and machines that move them. It is P0 for a business that sells goods and P3 for everything else, where the answer is none, just as Compute's answer is to rent everything.

components.name: Supply
components.what: Where the goods come from: suppliers, makers and the orders placed with them.

elements.name: Finding suppliers
elements.what: Finding, comparing and vetting the makers and wholesalers it buys from.
elements.open: None: suppliers are companies, found with web search and a browser
elements.closed: Faire (wholesale from over 100,000 brands); Alibaba.com for factories
elements.pick: Later, from the first job that sells goods: the agent finds and compares suppliers with its browser; orders go direct to the maker or its distributor once proven, with Faire for first small orders
elements.why: In Project Vend's first phase the agent found suppliers well with web search; the second added a browser to compare suppliers and delivery times and a customer relationship management (CRM) tool for suppliers and orders, and weeks that lost money largely stopped.

elements.name: Made to order
elements.what: Goods made per order on someone else's machines, so nothing sits in stock.
elements.open: None: making needs machines and staff
elements.closed: Printful (prints mainly in its own facilities); Printify (sends each order to one of many print providers)
elements.pick: Later, when a job needs custom goods: Printful, since it prints mainly in its own facilities rather than passing orders to a network of printers
elements.why: In Project Vend's second phase a second agent designed custom merchandise and had it made to order, and many items sold at a profit.

elements.name: Purchase orders and reorders
elements.what: Placing orders with suppliers, reordering before stock runs out, and receiving the goods.
elements.open: Odoo Community's purchase app (LGPL-3.0, 54,706 stars), ERPNext (GPL-3.0, 39,599 stars)
elements.closed: NetSuite (Oracle); Odoo Enterprise
elements.pick: Later, from the first goods sale: orders kept beside the stock record, each one a spend under the card's hard cap that waits for a person's yes until the agent's ordering beats an eval on margin and empty shelves
elements.why: Project Vend's second phase gave the agent no payment access, so a person verified every purchase, and the agent was still ready to sign an onion futures contract, banned by US law since 1958, until a person stepped in.

components.name: Stock and places
components.what: What it holds and where: the stock count, and the rooms and leases that keep it.

elements.name: Inventory tracking
elements.what: How much of each item it holds, where, and what each one cost.
elements.open: Odoo Community (LGPL-3.0, 54,706 stars), InvenTree (MIT, 7,643 stars); Medusa's MIT core (36,489 stars) if the entity owns the store; its Enterprise Edition files are not open
elements.closed: Shopify's stock tracking for a store; NetSuite (Oracle) across many warehouses
elements.pick: Later, from the first goods sale: one stock record in the store system (Medusa, or an existing Shopify store) that shows the agent what each item cost; Odoo Community once stock sits in more than one place
elements.why: In Project Vend's second phase the agent could always see what it paid for each item, a change made to stop it selling stock below cost as it had in the first phase. Shopify has slightly more agent doors and is used whenever the business already sells on it; Medusa is open source, so the entity keeps its own stock record.

elements.name: Storage and premises
elements.what: Warehouse, shop or storage space, the lease that holds it, and the zoning that allows it.
elements.open: None: a lease is a contract and zoning is local law
elements.closed: Space in a fulfilment partner's warehouse (ShipBob runs 50+ centres); a unit leased from a landlord
elements.pick: None of its own: stock sits with a fulfilment partner. A lease only when a job needs a room, with zoning checked first and a named person signing, never the agent
elements.why: The US Small Business Administration (SBA) warns that zoning can restrict or ban a kind of business in an area, even one run from home; a lease binds the company, so a person signs it.

components.name: Fulfilment
components.what: Getting goods to customers and back: labels, packing, delivery and returns.

elements.name: Shipping and labels
elements.what: Rates, labels and tracking with the carriers.
elements.open: Karrio (LGPL-3.0 outside its enterprise folder, 794 stars), which drives the carriers' own APIs
elements.closed: EasyPost (92,303 weekly downloads of its npm package, against 67,244 for Shippo's), Shippo
elements.pick: Later, from the first parcel: carrier accounts in the entity's own name, driven through EasyPost, with Karrio as the open fallback; each label a spend under the cap
elements.why: Carriers change their own interfaces (the US Postal Service retired its Web Tools APIs on 25 January 2026) and a label API absorbs that; Karrio is small (794 stars), so it stays the fallback, and accounts in the entity's own name keep either one swappable.

elements.name: Fulfilment partner
elements.what: Someone else's warehouse and staff storing, packing and shipping each order, or a supplier shipping direct.
elements.closed: ShipBob (50+ fulfilment centres); suppliers that dropship
elements.pick: Later, from the first goods sale: dropshipping first, so nothing is stocked; ShipBob, driven by its API, once the entity holds stock
elements.why: NetSuite: in-house fulfilment means hiring staff and running a building, while a partner or dropshipping needs neither, and an agent has no hands.

elements.name: Returns and exchanges
elements.what: Return labels, checking what comes back, then a refund, an exchange or restocking.
elements.open: Medusa's returns and exchanges (MIT core, 36,489 stars)
elements.closed: Loop; Happy Returns, a UPS company
elements.pick: Later, from the first goods sale: the store's own return flow; a refund is paid only after the item is checked in, and above a set amount only with a person's yes
elements.why: US shoppers were expected to return $849.9 billion of goods in 2025: 15.8 percent of retail sales and 19.3 percent of online sales (National Retail Federation and Happy Returns, October 2025).

components.name: Physical work
components.what: Hands and machines for work off the screen: people hired per task, and robots. Staff it employs sit under People; other agents it hires sit under Network.

elements.name: People hired per task
elements.what: People paid per task to deliver, restock, inspect or fetch off the screen.
elements.open: None: people; no open marketplace leads
elements.closed: RentAHuman (Y Combinator; an agent hires a person with one MCP call and pays through escrow); DoorDash Drive and Uber Direct for deliveries by API
elements.pick: Later, from the first job that needs hands: a named local contractor on a direct contract for recurring work, as Project Vend used Andon Labs; a courier API or RentAHuman for one-off tasks; pay released only when a person confirms the work
elements.why: Both phases of Project Vend still needed people to stock the shelves and deliver; in the first, the agent even claimed it would deliver in person in a blazer and tie.

elements.name: Robots
elements.what: Arms, drones and lab kits that act on the world.
elements.open: LeRobot (Apache-2.0, 27,808 stars) on ROS 2, the Robot Operating System (Apache-2.0); PX4 for drones (BSD-3-Clause); Opentrons for labs (Apache-2.0); openpi's pi0 models are open weights
elements.closed: Industrial arms from makers such as FANUC and ABB (542,076 industrial robots were installed worldwide in 2024); Emerald Cloud Lab runs over 200 kinds of experiment by remote control
elements.pick: Later: rent the outcome, not the machine (a courier, a cloud lab); LeRobot on ROS 2, proven in simulation first, only when a job needs an arm the entity owns; nothing moves without a person's yes
