elements.why: Physical acts cannot be undone. A simulator such as robosuite (MIT) can lift a cube on 2 CPUs, while WetRobo's lab arm kit can go no further without the hardware.

components.name: Product safety
components.what: Keeping what it sells safe: cover when a product causes harm, the rules goods must meet, and recalls. Licences and permits sit under Company.

elements.name: Product liability cover
elements.what: Insurance for injury or damage caused by a product it sells; the company's other cover sits under Company.
elements.closed: Chubb, Hiscox, Liberty Mutual and NEXT Insurance, the panel Marsh and Amazon chose for Amazon sellers
elements.pick: Later, before the first physical product ships: product liability cover from one of those insurers, sized to what each marketplace requires
elements.why: The US Small Business Administration (SBA) lists product liability cover for any business that makes, wholesales, distributes or sells a product; Amazon requires it within 30 days of passing $10,000 in sales in one month.

elements.name: Safety standards and recalls
elements.what: The safety rules its goods must meet, the certificates that prove it, and pulling recalled goods.
elements.open: None: the standards are law; recalls from the US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) are open data through its API
elements.closed: Testing labs such as UL Solutions, Intertek and SGS
elements.pick: Later, from the first physical product: sell only goods whose maker supplies the required certificate, and name a responsible person before selling in the European Union (EU); check stock against the CPSC's recalls daily and pull any match at once
elements.why: Since 8 July 2026 regulated US imports must file their certificate electronically; the EU's General Product Safety Regulation has applied since 13 December 2024 and needs a responsible person in the EU; the CPSC listed 459 recalls from 1 January to 24 September 2026.

components.name: Sensors
components.what: Sensors, cameras and building systems in its own places, read as inputs. Evolution's physical-world signals are the same readings used to improve the work; Surfaces' devices are what people wear or carry to use it.

elements.name: Sensors and cameras
elements.what: Sensors and cameras in its own places, such as stock levels, temperatures and doors, read as inputs.
elements.open: Home Assistant (Apache-2.0, 91,178 stars); Frigate for cameras (MIT, 36,140 stars)
elements.closed: Samsara ($1.9 billion in annual recurring revenue, fiscal 2026); AWS IoT
elements.pick: Later, read-only by default, when an agent runs a physical place: Home Assistant as the hub, each reading written into the trace as an event
elements.why: Read-only by default is the safe method for these inputs: a machine completes work only under a rule the buyer approved in advance.

elements.name: Building systems
elements.what: Heating, locks, alarms and access control, read through the building's own system.
elements.closed: Johnson Controls, Siemens and Honeywell building platforms
elements.pick: Later, when an agent works in a managed building: read through the building's own system, read-only; a command to a lock, a door or the heating waits for a person's yes
elements.why: Safety-critical physical systems stay read-only: a wrong command to a lock or the heating harms people, not just data.

categories.name: Trust
categories.question: Why can anyone rely on it?
categories.what: Verifying every output, the controls around every action, security, the records it leaves, privacy and compliance. Verification is the part nobody has solved; it lives here.

components.name: Verification
components.what: Whatever says the work was right: a rule, a decision model, a person, an expert.

elements.name: Rule verifiers
elements.what: Deterministic verifiers that never need a model.
elements.open: Zod and JSON Schema; Open Policy Agent
elements.closed: None worth naming
elements.pick: Schemas and rule files, verified before anything leaves
elements.why: The cheapest verifier never needs a model.

elements.name: Decision-model verifiers
elements.what: The checklist run on every output in one call.
elements.open: A frontier model as judge (deepeval, Inspect)
elements.closed: Jev
elements.pick: Jev, confirmed on about 200 held-back cases per decision: made-up ones first, then real de-identified ones; with health data, only under a signed business associate agreement
elements.why: One call runs the checklist on every output. Made-up cases are only a start: 60 cases cannot tell 97% from 99%, so real held-back cases decide.

elements.name: Human review queue
elements.what: Uncertain cases routed to a person, whose answer becomes training.
elements.closed: gotoHuman
elements.pick: Answers the verifier is unsure of (scored between 0.3 and 0.7) go to a person; each answer becomes a labelled case in the pool (Evolution: Signals)
elements.why: The person sees only what the verifier cannot settle, and every answer grows the held-back set the next eval runs on.

elements.name: Expert sign-off
elements.what: A named expert signs the work in regulated jobs.
elements.open: The entity's own experts at the edge
elements.closed: Expert marketplaces (Mercor, Surge AI)
elements.pick: A named senior person on the customer's staff signs off on the routine work; specialists sign off on their own cases (their contracts and pay: People: Experts at the edge)
elements.why: In regulated work a named person must stand behind the output.

components.name: Controls
components.what: Limits on what it may do, and who must say yes.

elements.name: Permissions
elements.what: Least agency: each tool and each account scoped to the job.
elements.closed: Microsoft Entra Agent ID, Okta for AI agents
elements.pick: Scoped per job and written into the contract; revoked when the job ends
elements.why: Least agency: an agent never holds more access than the person it acts for.

elements.name: Approvals
elements.what: A person says yes to anything risky or leaving the building.
elements.closed: gotoHuman
elements.pick: A hard stop before anything that signs, pays or sends, unless a standing rule the owner approved covers that kind of act; signing always needs a person, and so does a payment above the owner's line. No answer means no
elements.why: Every act that cannot be undone goes through it or through a rule a person approved, and an approval nobody answers does nothing.

elements.name: Spending caps
elements.what: Hard limits at the payment rail and in the grade.
elements.open: None: enforced by the card network
elements.closed: Card issuers' controls (Ramp, Stripe Issuing, Mercury)
elements.pick: The rule: a cap per agent, sized by its grade and enforced at the payment rail (Money: Accounts) and on compute (Operations: Cost control)
elements.why: A limit the card network enforces cannot be talked around.

elements.name: Autonomy ladder
elements.what: How far it may act alone, per kind of action: watch, suggest, propose, act with a veto, act and report. A run of verified approvals moves it up; any miss moves it down.
elements.closed: None worth naming
elements.pick: The ladder, per action and per agent: signing never climbs past propose, paying climbs only below the owner's line, and sending can climb under a standing rule
elements.why: Autonomy is earned per action, never granted to an agent as a whole.

elements.name: Kill switch
elements.what: One control that stops everything, on the owner's side.
elements.closed: Microsoft Agent 365 (a registry that can stop every agent)
elements.pick: An in-house stop: one call revokes the agent's keys, turns off its flag and ends its runs
elements.why: Firing an agent takes one action: it empties the agent's grants, zeroes its spending cap and leaves a marker that every gate checks first, so the agent can no longer take work, delegate, send or spend. Enterprise buyers expect one place to see and stop every agent.

elements.name: Recourse
elements.what: Anyone affected by what it did can contest the outcome and reach a person, on any channel at any step; staff and experts can raise a concern about it, anonymously if they wish.
elements.open: GlobaLeaks (AGPL-3.0, 1,517 stars) for the anonymous concerns channel; contests run through the entity's own review queue
elements.closed: Hosted ethics lines such as NAVEX EthicsPoint; for customer contests, the help desk under Support
elements.pick: 'Talk to a person' works on every channel at every step and hands the case, with its history, to a staff member. Anyone affected can contest any decision or refusal; each contest is logged, answered within two working days and counted on the record, and an upheld one becomes a held-back case. Inside, a named address and an anonymous form reach a founder who does not own that agent; GlobaLeaks when the team needs a formal channel.
elements.why: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework asks for ways for users and affected people to report problems and appeal outcomes (MEASURE 3.3), and for appeal and override in monitoring plans (MANAGE 4.1); ISO/IEC 42001 asks for a way to report concerns (A.3). A contest that reaches a person also catches what the verifiers missed.

elements.name: Callers it lets in
elements.what: Who may call an entity's MCP server, API and agent card, with what scopes and limits.
elements.open: The MCP authorization specification (OAuth 2.1); Supabase Auth's OAuth 2.1 server and Better Auth's MCP plugin, each of which signs MCP callers in; Upstash's rate limiter
elements.closed: Clerk, WorkOS AuthKit and Stytch Connected Apps, each of which can sign callers in to your own MCP server
elements.pick: Every door signs its callers in: OAuth 2.1 on the MCP server, as the MCP specification requires, with the product's own sign-in service (Software: Accounts and payments) handing out the tokens, and a key per caller on the API; scopes per tool, limits per caller (Upstash), and every call written to the record; an unknown agent gets only public, read-only tools
elements.why: Other agents calling the entity is half of the model, and nothing else decides who may. The sign-in service a product already runs can sign these callers in (Supabase Auth has an OAuth 2.1 server for MCP, Better Auth an MCP plugin), so no second service is needed. Limits per caller stop one agent from spending another's budget, and the record shows who called what.

components.name: Security
components.what: Keeping secrets secret and instructions honest.

elements.name: Secrets keeper
elements.what: Where keys live, rotated and injected at run time, never in a prompt.
elements.closed: 1Password, HashiCorp Vault (now under a licence that is not open source, the BSL), Doppler
elements.pick: Infisical as the store, with Infisical's open-source Agent Vault as the broker that attaches keys on the way out
elements.why: Storing a key and letting a model use it without reading it are two jobs; 1Password and Naive now sell the second. Agent Vault, open source since March 2026, is such a broker: a proxy that adds the real key to allowed calls, revocable per session. 1Password is the runner-up: its broker is a preview for Business customers and its MCP server a desktop experiment.

elements.name: Prompt-injection defence
elements.what: Spotting instructions planted in untrusted input.
elements.open: NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails. Meta's Llama Prompt Guard is open weights under Meta's licence, not open source
elements.closed: Lakera (Check Point), Protect AI (Palo Alto Networks)
elements.pick: Jev as a verifier before each tool call; with health data, only under a signed business associate agreement
elements.why: Verifying each tool call before it runs stops a planted instruction before it can act.

elements.name: Red-teaming and scanning
elements.what: Attacking it before others do: planted instructions, data theft, tool misuse.
elements.closed: Lakera (Check Point), Protect AI (Palo Alto Networks)
elements.pick: promptfoo red-team runs in CI, pinned to a version
elements.why: OpenAI announced on 9 March 2026 that it would buy promptfoo and keep it open source; pin the version and watch the licence.

elements.name: Supply chain
elements.what: Third-party code, skills and hooks installed only in isolation.
elements.closed: Snyk (with Invariant), Socket
elements.pick: Third-party skills, hooks and servers installed only in a sandbox, after a scan
elements.why: Only about half of listed MCP servers complete a handshake, and one scanner gave a setup with a hidden key only a C, not a fail.

elements.name: Staff access and devices
elements.what: Single sign-on and two-factor sign-in for every person with access, secured laptops and phones, a regular review of who can reach what, and access removed the day someone leaves. Vendor staff who touch its systems are logged too.
elements.open: Keycloak (Apache 2.0, 37,017 stars) for single sign-on; Fleet (MIT outside its ee/ folder, 6,923 stars) on osquery (Apache 2.0 or GPL 2.0, 23,588 stars) for device checks
elements.closed: Okta (used by more than 20,000 customers, 2026); Google's Access Transparency and Access Approval, which log and gate Google staff access to its agent platform's runtime, sessions and memory
elements.pick: Google Workspace as the one staff sign-in, with passkeys or security keys required, and single sign-on from it wherever a tool offers it; two-factor sign-in on every tool that does not. Production keys stay in Infisical and nobody copies them out. The compliance tool's device agent checks disk encryption, screen lock and updates, and runs a quarterly access review and the leaver checklist. Vendor access logs turned on wherever offered. Okta and Fleet once the team outgrows a review done by hand, or a buyer requires them.
elements.why: Buyers' security questionnaires ask for two-factor sign-in, encryption and access reviews, and the Cloud Native Computing Foundation requires enforced access controls on a project's code, such as two-factor sign-in, before it can graduate.

elements.name: Security monitoring
elements.what: Watching live behaviour for attacks and for an agent acting outside its job: sign-ins from new places, denied tool calls, planted instructions, spending near a cap. Every alert reaches a named responder.
elements.open: Wazuh (GPL 2.0, 17,013 stars) for logs and alerts across machines and cloud accounts; Falco (Apache 2.0, 9,420 stars) for behaviour inside containers. Security Onion is under the Elastic License, so it is source-available, not open source
elements.closed: CrowdStrike Falcon, whose AI Detection and Response module watches AI use ($5.3 billion in annual recurring revenue at the end of fiscal 2026, up 24%); Microsoft Agent 365 with Defender for agents (out 1 May 2026, $15 per user a month)
elements.pick: Rules over the records the entity keeps anyway: the traces, the policy hook's denials, Jev's injection flags, the secrets broker's log and the card's declines, with any hit paging the same on-call phone as an outage. Turn on the alerts the code host and the cloud already offer. A managed detection service or a hosted SIEM (security information and event management) when a buyer asks for round-the-clock monitoring, or at the SOC 2 audit (an independent audit of a company's security controls).
elements.why: The 2026 list of agent risks from OWASP (the Open Worldwide Application Security Project) adds rogue agents (ASI10), agents acting beyond their objectives, and NIST's AI Risk Management Framework asks for monitoring plans that include incident response (MANAGE 4.1). The signals sit in the entity's own logs; a rule turns them into a page.

elements.name: Vulnerability disclosure
elements.what: A public, safe way for anyone to report a security hole, a named person who answers, and a promise of how fast.
elements.open: security.txt (RFC 9116, an Internet Engineering Task Force standard) on every domain; a SECURITY.md from the templates in the Open Source Security Foundation's (OpenSSF) disclosure guide (CC BY 4.0)
elements.closed: HackerOne ($81 million in bounties paid through it in 2025)
elements.pick: security.txt pointing to a monitored security address, and a SECURITY.md with GitHub's private vulnerability reporting turned on in every public repository; acknowledge within two working days, fix or explain within 90 days. A paid bug bounty only after the first penetration test and SOC 2, when someone can triage the reports.
elements.why: OpenSSF Scorecard marks down a project with no SECURITY.md, and since 11 September 2026 the EU Cyber Resilience Act makes makers of installable software sold in the EU report actively exploited holes, with a final report due 14 days after the fix.

elements.name: Encryption and customer-held keys
elements.what: Data encrypted in transit and at rest everywhere, the most sensitive fields encrypted again by the entity, and the buyer's own key when a contract asks for it.
elements.open: OpenBao (MPL 2.0, 8,131 stars; the open fork of Vault), whose transit engine encrypts fields without the app holding the key; age (BSD 3-Clause) and SOPS (MPL 2.0) for files
elements.closed: Google Cloud KMS and AWS KMS (key management services); Google's agent platform takes customer-managed keys for its runtime, sessions and memory
elements.pick: Encryption in transit and the providers' encryption at rest by default (Supabase, Cloudflare R2, the model providers). With health data, patient identifiers encrypted again with one key per customer in a cloud key service that the app can use but never read out, so a copied database is unreadable. Customer-held keys when a buyer's contract asks; OpenBao once the entity runs its own servers.
elements.why: Under the HIPAA breach rule, health data encrypted to the US health department's (HHS) guidance is not 'unsecured', so losing it does not trigger breach notices; buyers' questionnaires ask for encryption beside two-factor sign-in and access reviews.

elements.name: Fraud and abuse prevention
elements.what: Stopping spam, fake sign-ups, stolen cards, bots, and people who talk the agent into refunds, discounts or free work.
elements.open: Osprey (Apache 2.0), the rules engine Discord built against spam and bots, now developed in the open by ROOST (Robust Open Online Safety Tools) and used by Bluesky; ALTCHA (MIT, 2,781 stars) to challenge bots on forms; the disposable-email-domains list (CC0). Marble's fraud engine is under the Elastic License, so it is source-available, not open source
elements.closed: Stripe Radar (a 32% average cut in fraud, trained on Stripe's network, which processed $1.9 trillion in 2025; it also flags free-trial abuse and tells bad bots from agent purchases)
elements.pick: Stripe Radar on every card payment when Stripe is the processor; ALTCHA and the disposable-email list on public sign-up forms; per-caller rate limits in Upstash. Discounts, refunds and free work come only from a rule table, and anything above a set amount goes for approval. Osprey once there are enough users to write rules against.
elements.why: In Anthropic's Project Vend (June 2025) customers talked the shop agent into discount codes and free items, including a 25% staff discount when 99% of its customers were staff. A rule the agent cannot argue with, plus a model that scores every payment, closes both doors.

elements.name: Penetration test and vulnerability scans
elements.what: An outside firm attacks the product at least once a year and automated scans run more often, with findings fixed on a deadline and a summary shared with buyers.
elements.open: ZAP (Apache 2.0, 15,838 stars) and Nuclei (MIT, 31,577 stars) for automated scans; the test itself is a service
elements.closed: An independent testing firm, chosen per test; a paid bug bounty later (Trust: Vulnerability disclosure)
elements.pick: An independent penetration test of the product, its doors (API, MCP server, CLI) and its agent paths (planted instructions, tool misuse) before the first real customer data and every 12 months after; automated scans at least monthly; findings that matter fixed within 90 days; the summary letter on the trust page
elements.why: MVSP, the baseline for enterprise-ready products written with Google, Salesforce, Okta and others, asks for a penetration test by a security vendor at least once a year and fixes within 90 days. HHS's proposed update to the HIPAA Security Rule (27 December 2024) would require vulnerability scans every 6 months and a penetration test every 12 months; HHS's page still describes it as proposed (read 27 September 2026).

components.name: Safety
components.what: Keeping what it says, and what people send through it, safe for everyone it serves, children included.

elements.name: Harmful output and misuse filtering
elements.what: Refusing harmful requests and blocking harmful answers on every surface, going in and coming out, against a policy written for the job.
elements.open: gpt-oss-safeguard (OpenAI, Apache 2.0 weights; 38,209 downloads of the 20-billion-parameter model in 30 days), which reads a written policy at run time; Qwen3Guard (Apache 2.0); NeMo Guardrails (Apache 2.0) to wire them in. Llama Guard 4 and ShieldGemma are open weights under Meta's and Google's own licences, not open source
elements.closed: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (AWS says it blocks up to 88% of harmful content); the model providers' own safety training
elements.pick: The frontier model's own refusals, then gpt-oss-safeguard verifying what goes in and what comes out against the entity's written policy; with health data, hosted under a business associate agreement before any patient text reaches it. In health care the first rule is fixed, not generated: a message that describes an emergency (chest pain, fainting, trouble breathing) gets a set reply to call 911 and pages a person, and the agent never gives medical advice.
elements.why: People probe a new agent at once: in Anthropic's Project Vend (June 2025) staff immediately asked the shop agent for sensitive items and for instructions for harmful substances. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework asks that a system fail safely (MEASURE 2.6), and a line patients call will hear emergencies, where only a fixed reply is safe.

elements.name: Reports and moderation
elements.what: Report, block and human review for anything people can post or send through it, and a published way to reach the operator.
elements.open: Coop (Apache 2.0) from ROOST (Robust Open Online Safety Tools), a review console with queues, routing and enforcement rules, used in production by Notion; Ozone (Bluesky, MIT or Apache 2.0); Meta's Hasher-Matcher-Actioner in ThreatExchange (BSD) for matching known abuse images
elements.closed: Hive's moderation models, priced per use; the moderation filters in the big clouds, such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
elements.pick: A report and a block control wherever people can post or message, with reports and the verifier's flags landing in the human review queue and answered within one working day. A one-to-one service, such as a scheduling line, needs only block, report and a published contact; Coop once people can publish to each other.
elements.why: Apple's App Review Guidelines (1.2) require every app with user content to filter objectionable material, take reports with timely responses, block abusive users and publish contact details. Coop, open since February 2026, gives a small team a free review console with child-safety workflows built in.

elements.name: Minors and age assurance
elements.what: Knowing when a user may be a child, and changing what it collects, shows and does for them: a parent's consent, no tracking, a person in the loop.
elements.open: None: age assurance rests on app-store signals and identity checks, not on code anyone can run
elements.closed: Apple's Declared Age Range API and Google Play's age signals, which state app-store laws now lean on: Texas's App Store Accountability Act applies to new Apple accounts after a court lifted its injunction, and California, Louisiana and Utah laws take effect in 2026 and 2027
elements.pick: In health care the agent follows the customer's own rules for minors, which usually route through the parent or guardian on file, and never gathers a child's details on its own. Consumer products say 18 and over in their terms and read the app store's age signal wherever an app ships; anything aimed at children waits for a lawyer and for verified parental consent.
elements.why: The Federal Trade Commission's amended children's privacy rule (COPPA) took effect on 23 June 2025 with compliance due by 22 April 2026, and Apple's guideline 1.2.1(a) already requires age limits based on verified or declared age for creator content.

components.name: Records
components.what: What it did, kept so anyone can verify.

elements.name: Audit log
elements.what: An append-only log of every action that moved money or changed state.
elements.open: Langfuse traces. immudb moved to the Business Source License, so it is source-available
elements.closed: WorkOS Audit Logs
elements.pick: An append-only table plus the traces
elements.why: An append-only log of every grant, cap, firing and edit lets anyone verify what happened.

elements.name: The record
elements.what: The verified history of its work for one customer, which belongs to that customer, and the scorecard the buyer sees from it: the share an expert signed off, the cost per signed-off piece, one weekly number that improves without a person.
elements.closed: None: nobody sells a verified work record
elements.pick: An in-house record
elements.why: Trust lets a customer hand over more.

elements.name: System card
elements.what: One public page per agent: what it is for and not for, what it runs on, how it scores on held-back cases, its known failures, and what a person verifies.
elements.open: CHAI's Applied Model Card (Coalition for Health AI), a free template and schema under a permissive licence, built to support the US health IT transparency rule (HTI-1)
elements.closed: None worth naming: frontier labs publish system cards for their own models, not for what others build on them
elements.pick: A CHAI-format card per agent, generated from its contract and its latest held-back results so it never drifts, published on the trust page with links to the cards of the models it runs on.
elements.why: Health AI makers now publish these 'nutrition labels': CHAI opened a public registry of them on 27 August 2026. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework asks that knowledge limits and human oversight be written down (MAP 2.2).

elements.name: Content credentials
elements.what: Machine-readable marks on every image, sound and video it makes, and a visible notice on anything that could pass for a real person or event.
elements.open: C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity), an open standard, with the c2pa-rs library (MIT or Apache 2.0); Google's SynthID Text (Apache 2.0) for text; Meta's AudioSeal and Video Seal (MIT)
elements.closed: Google SynthID (over 100 billion images and videos and 60,000 years of audio watermarked)
elements.pick: A C2PA manifest on every generated image, clip and video, naming the agent and the model, with any provider watermark left intact, and a visible AI label on synthetic voices and faces. Calls open by saying the caller is an AI (AI rules); media marks start with the first agent that publishes images, audio or video.
elements.why: Article 50 of the EU AI Act has applied since 2 August 2026: systems that generate audio, images, video or text must mark their output in a machine-readable, detectable way, and deep fakes must be disclosed. The EU's Digital Omnibus amendments deferred only certain specific duties, and the Commission's code of practice shows how to comply.

components.name: Privacy
components.what: What it may see, keep and share.

elements.name: Sensitive data handling
elements.what: Keeping personal and business-confidential data out of logs, prompts and tools that do not need it.
elements.closed: Private AI, Skyflow, Google Cloud Sensitive Data Protection
elements.pick: Presidio at every boundary: logs, prompts and exports
elements.why: Personal data that never enters a prompt cannot leak from it.

elements.name: Data residency
elements.what: Where data is stored and processed, pinned to a region when a law or a buyer requires it.
elements.closed: Region pinning on every major cloud and model provider
elements.pick: US regions by default; pinned per contract
elements.why: A residency law is one of the three reasons to own compute.

elements.name: Data rights
elements.what: Written permission for anything it keeps, per contract.
elements.closed: None: a contract clause
elements.pick: Contract clause per customer
elements.why: In healthcare the record belongs to the health system, so the contract asks explicitly.

elements.name: Retention and deletion
elements.what: How long each customer's data is kept, and deleting it on request.
elements.closed: None: a policy
elements.pick: A retention window per customer and a way to delete on request, before any real customer data
elements.why: Without a window, nothing is ever deleted and a deletion request has nowhere to go.

elements.name: Consent records
elements.what: What each person agreed to and when: how their data is used, sharing it with named AI vendors, and calls and texts. Verified before every use and revocable at any time.
elements.open: None maintained for consent records: Ethyca has archived Fides (Apache 2.0), whose last release was on 1 June 2026. CookieConsent (MIT, 5,686 stars) covers website cookie banners only
elements.closed: OneTrust consent and preferences, across web, mobile and connected TV
elements.pick: One consent table in the database: the person, the purpose (data use, a named AI vendor, calls, texts), the words they saw, the channel, the time and any withdrawal. Every call, text and vendor hand-off checks it first, and a STOP reply or a spoken 'stop calling' withdraws consent at once. In health care, patient data reaches a vendor under a business associate agreement, not consent; consent covers calls, texts and any use beyond the patient's care.
elements.why: The Federal Communications Commission ruled on 8 February 2024 that AI-generated voices are 'artificial' under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, and breaking that Act costs $500 to $1,500 per unwanted call or text. Apple's App Review Guidelines (5.1.2(i)) also require explicit permission before personal data is shared with third-party AI.

elements.name: Incident and breach notices
elements.what: Telling customers, affected people and regulators what happened, each on its deadline, when data leaks or an incident harms someone.
elements.open: PagerDuty's incident response guide (Apache 2.0) for the process; the deadlines are law and contract, not code
elements.closed: Breach counsel and forensics through the cyber insurer's panel; the online breach report of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for health data
elements.pick: A written breach runbook beside the on-call one: who decides, who writes, who tells whom, by when. With patient data the entity is the health-care customer's business associate: it tells that customer without unreasonable delay, within the clock their agreement sets and never later than the law's 60 days, and names each affected patient; the customer tells patients, HHS and, above 500 people in a state, the media. Other customers get the notice their data processing agreement promises. Rehearse it once before any real customer data.
elements.why: The HIPAA breach rule gives a business associate at most 60 days from discovery to tell the health-care provider, gives patients the same 60-day limit, and sends breaches of 500 or more to HHS within 60 days; data encrypted to its guidance is exempt. Healthcare breaches cost the most of any industry in IBM's 2025 report, $7.42 million on average.

elements.name: Access and export requests
elements.what: A person or a customer asks for a copy of everything held about them, or an export to take elsewhere: find it in every store and hand it over in a usable form, on deadline.
elements.open: None maintained: Ethyca has archived Fides (Apache 2.0), the open privacy-request engine, whose last release was on 1 June 2026. At small scale an export script over the entity's own stores does the job
elements.closed: OneTrust (privacy, consent and AI governance in one platform)
elements.pick: For patients the health-care customer answers, since HIPAA makes it responsible; the entity returns everything it holds on a patient within five working days of that customer's request, as an electronic copy, from one export script that searches the database, traces, memory and files by patient. The same script serves other customers' exports and their users' requests.
elements.why: HIPAA gives patients a right to a copy: the health-care provider must act within 30 days, with one 30-day extension, in the electronic form asked for when it can be produced. Deletion on request sits under Retention and deletion.

elements.name: Data map and risk analysis
elements.what: A list of every kind of sensitive data the product handles and a diagram of where it enters, which vendor sees it and where it rests, with a written risk analysis against it, reviewed at least yearly.
elements.open: Diagrams as code in the repo (Mermaid, MIT, 90,448 stars); the traces show every store an agent touched
elements.closed: Privacy platforms such as OneTrust (privacy, consent and AI governance); the SOC 2 compliance tool (Vanta or Drata) holds the risk assessment
elements.pick: Before real customer data: one list of data types (such as patient identifiers, call audio, card data, keys) and one diagram per product, generated from the vendor list and the traces where possible; with health data, the HIPAA risk analysis written against it and redone every year and after any new vendor or model
elements.why: HIPAA's Security Rule requires an accurate and thorough assessment of the risks to electronic patient data, and HHS's proposed update would require a technology asset inventory and a network map of how that data moves, at least every 12 months. MVSP asks every enterprise vendor for a list of sensitive data types and an up-to-date data-flow diagram.

components.name: Compliance
components.what: The paperwork buyers and laws require.

elements.name: Security certification (SOC 2 or ISO 27001)
elements.what: The audit health systems and enterprises ask vendors for.
elements.closed: Vanta, Drata
elements.pick: MVSP (Minimum Viable Secure Product) as the baseline before the audit; then Vanta or Drata, with an independent audit firm
elements.why: $25,000 to $50,000 in the first year and three to four months to a first report; never the compliance tool's own auditor (in March 2026 a leak alleged that Delve's audit reports were not genuine). MVSP says smaller companies not yet ready for SOC 2 can measure themselves against it. Vanta is the more used and Drata the more agent-usable (a hosted MCP server, where Vanta's is in beta and for admins only); both sell by quote, so the price on the day decides.

elements.name: Health data rules (HIPAA)
elements.what: Business associate agreements before any patient data.
elements.closed: Every vendor that could see patient data must sign
elements.pick: Signed before real patient data
elements.why: List every vendor that could see patient data and sign each agreement before the first record; Common Paper publishes a template.

elements.name: Rules of the vertical
elements.what: The job's own regulator, such as the FDA's rules for clinical software in healthcare.
elements.closed: Each vertical's regulator
elements.pick: In health care, scheduling and admin sit outside the FDA's rules; any agent that suggests a clinical order is verified by a lawyer first
elements.why: The FDA revised its clinical decision support guidance in January 2026.

elements.name: Agent certification
elements.what: A standard written for AI agents that a buyer can verify.
elements.closed: AIUC-1 (Sierra certified, September 2026)
elements.pick: AIUC-1 for agents sold to health systems
elements.why: The first standard written for agents; health systems will ask.

elements.name: Being buyable
elements.what: The security questionnaire, the list of subprocessors and a public trust page; the data processing agreement itself is under Company: Legal.
elements.closed: Vanta Trust Center, SafeBase (Drata)
elements.pick: A trust page with the list of subprocessors and a standard questionnaire, kept in the compliance tool
elements.why: A health system asks for these before it signs.

elements.name: AI rules
elements.what: Laws on AI systems, such as the EU AI Act.
elements.closed: The EU AI Act; US state AI laws
elements.pick: Disclose AI in every reply and bio; keep the event log high-risk rules ask for
elements.why: Admin work is unlikely to count as high-risk, but health and hiring decisions can, and the log costs little.

elements.name: AI risk management
elements.what: A register of what could go wrong with each agent, an impact assessment before it acts on people, and the management system buyers verify: the NIST AI Risk Management Framework now, ISO/IEC 42001 when asked.
elements.open: The AI Risk Management Framework from NIST, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (free, and a framework, not software); CISO Assistant (AGPL-3.0 outside its enterprise folder, 4,460 stars) ships it with ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act among 200+ frameworks
elements.closed: ISO/IEC 42001 certification by an accredited auditor (Anthropic holds it, certified by Schellman; more than 350 organisations held it by April 2026, by one outside count); Vanta automates the evidence
elements.pick: Map each agent to the NIST framework in the SOC 2 compliance tool: a risk register, an impact assessment before any agent decides about people, and a yearly review. ISO/IEC 42001 after SOC 2, when a buyer asks; the same tool maps both.
elements.why: NIST asks for risk work sized to a stated risk tolerance and for impacts on people to be assessed (GOVERN 1.3, MAP 5.1); ISO/IEC 42001 turns this into 38 auditable controls, impact assessment among them (A.5), and buyers' certification path runs SOC 2 and ISO 27001 first, the AI standard next.

elements.name: Vendor review
elements.what: Checking every model and data provider before it sees anything, and again after each model change: its terms, whether it trains on the entity's data, how long it keeps it, where it runs, its audit report and a signed agreement.
elements.open: The Cloud Security Alliance's AI Controls Matrix v1.1 and its AI questionnaire, AI-CAIQ (free frameworks, not software; 22 June 2026, 320 questions); CISO Assistant's third-party risk module (AGPL-3.0)
elements.closed: Vanta's vendor risk management, inside the compliance tool (Vanta passed $300 million in yearly revenue by April 2026)
elements.pick: One vendor list that is also the trust page's subprocessor list and the business associate agreement list. Before use: terms read, training on the entity's data off, the shortest retention offered, region, audit report and signed agreement on file. After each model change: re-run the held-back cases and re-read the terms, because a new model version is a new vendor decision.
elements.why: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework asks for policies on third-party AI risk and for pre-trained models to be monitored (GOVERN 6.1, MANAGE 3.2), and ISO/IEC 42001 covers suppliers (A.10); in health care no vendor may see patient data before its business associate agreement is signed.

elements.name: Platform rules
elements.what: The terms of every channel, store and provider it depends on, who re-reads them, and the fallback when one shuts it out.
elements.open: None: each platform writes its own terms. Channels no single company controls, such as email on the entity's own domain and its own web chat, are the fallback
elements.closed: Meta's WhatsApp Business terms; Apple's and Google's store rules; X's automation rules; US carriers' registration for business texts (10DLC); each model provider's usage policy
elements.pick: A register of every channel and provider, the clause that could cut it off, an owner who re-reads it each quarter, and a second channel wired before launch (a text or email behind every WhatsApp or iMessage flow). The texting registration (the 10DLC brand and campaign) and Meta's business verification are done once per company through Telnyx, with the company's legal name, tax number and address first. On WhatsApp the agent acts as a business's own customer-service agent, which the 2026 ban did not target.
elements.why: Meta changed WhatsApp's Business terms on 15 October 2025 and shut general-purpose AI assistants out from 15 January 2026, let them back for a fee in March 2026, and was ordered by the European Commission in June 2026 to restore free access. A channel can close within weeks, so the fallback must already work. The texting registration belongs to the company, not the customer, and takes one to two weeks, so start it early.

elements.name: Customer screening
elements.what: Checking customers and payees against sanctions and export lists in each market it sells into, and verifying who they are wherever money moves.
elements.open: Moov Watchman (Apache 2.0): the US Treasury's sanctions lists (OFAC), the US Consolidated Screening List (which carries the export lists), and EU, UK and UN lists, with 0.99 precision on 472,477 labelled names. OpenSanctions' code is MIT but its data is CC BY-NC 4.0, so commercial use needs a paid licence
elements.closed: Persona for know-your-customer (KYC) and know-your-business (KYB) checks, now sold for the owners of agent funds; Stripe Connect verifies the accounts it pays out to (11 million onboarded)
elements.pick: While Stripe moves the money, its checks on payers and on the payees paid through Connect do the know-your-customer work. Add a sign-up block for comprehensively sanctioned countries and regions, and a Watchman check on each new business customer and each expert the entity pays; Persona only when an entity must verify people itself.
elements.why: Sanctions and export lists apply per market even to software sold online, and wherever an agent moves money the owners of the funds must pass KYC and KYB checks.

elements.name: Open-source trust signals
elements.what: For an entity that is an open-source project: the public scores and badges that tell users its code is maintained and safe to depend on.
elements.open: OpenSSF (Open Source Security Foundation) Scorecard (Apache 2.0, 5,713 stars) run as a GitHub Action; the OpenSSF Best Practices badge (passing, silver, gold; its site's code is MIT); Sigstore's cosign (Apache 2.0) for signed releases
elements.closed: None that users see: the signals are public by design. Socket and Snyk score packages privately for their customers
elements.pick: Every public repository runs the Scorecard Action with its badge in the README, earns the passing Best Practices badge before a 1.0 release, signs releases with cosign, and keeps a SECURITY.md (see Vulnerability disclosure).
elements.why: Scorecard scans the 1 million most critical open-source projects every week and publishes the scores, so a project is graded whether or not it looks; the Cloud Native Computing Foundation requires the passing badge before a project can graduate.

categories.name: Operations
categories.question: How is it kept running?
categories.what: Where it runs, how changes ship, how failures are caught, what it costs, and how it starts, moves and retires.

components.name: Runtime
components.what: Where the entity's loop runs, always on.

elements.name: Always-on host
elements.what: Keeps the agent loop running between messages and across restarts.
elements.open: LangGraph, Letta, Cloudflare Agents SDK, self-hosted
elements.closed: Claude Managed Agents ($0.08 per session-hour, idle time free), OpenAI Agents API, Cloudflare
elements.pick: Claude Code on a subscription for internal work and every prototype; Claude Managed Agents for agents that serve customers, on an API account opened when the first customer signs
elements.why: Agents that serve customers run in the cloud, and Managed Agents costs the least to integrate. Its API account is the one place a per-token key is allowed, and only for a customer's live work.

elements.name: Durable execution
elements.what: Long jobs that survive crashes and resume where they stopped.
elements.open: Temporal, Vercel Workflows (Apache 2.0), Trigger.dev, Hatchet, DBOS; Restate is source-available (Business Source License), not open source
elements.closed: Temporal Cloud (Temporal was valued at $12.55 billion in September 2026), Inngest, Cloudflare Workflows
elements.pick: Trigger.dev for agent runs and app jobs; Temporal if a customer's workload outgrows it
elements.why: Each Trigger.dev task runs with no time limit, so an agent run of hours is one task, and the same tool runs app jobs. Temporal leads on use (4.63 million npm plus 8.30 million PyPI downloads a week, against 1.13 million) but needs its own cluster or Temporal Cloud; Vercel Workflows, generally available since 16 April 2026, runs inside Vercel's function limits.

elements.name: Provider limits and capacity
elements.what: What happens when a provider's limit is hit, and who gets capacity first.
elements.closed: Anthropic's priority tier, OpenRouter
elements.pick: Fallbacks through the gateway; on a hard limit, pause and resume, never quietly downgrade judgement work
elements.why: A hard limit, such as a plan's five-hour usage window, passes with time, while a quiet downgrade lowers the quality of judgement work.

elements.name: Load and capacity tests
elements.what: Proving the doors and the loop hold at a launch spike and at ten times today's work, before customers find the limit.
elements.open: k6 (AGPL 3.0, 31,668 stars; tests written in JavaScript); Locust (MIT, 28,183 stars, 2.2 million downloads a week; tests written in Python)
elements.closed: Grafana Cloud k6, BlazeMeter
elements.pick: k6 in CI (continuous integration) before each launch and before each new customer goes live, run against a stub model for volume plus a small sample of real model calls; plan capacity around the model provider's rate limit (Operations: Provider limits and capacity). AGPL is fine for a tool the entity runs and never ships
elements.why: Google's launch checklist asks for a load test, the launch spike and ten times growth. For an agent the first ceiling is usually the model provider's limit, and a full-scale test with real model calls costs real money, so the stub carries the volume.

components.name: Build tools
components.what: What builds and changes the entity: the coding harness, where its model calls come from, the code host, review and design tools.

elements.name: Coding harness
elements.what: The agent that writes and changes the code.
elements.closed: Claude Code
elements.pick: Claude Code
elements.why: A widely used coding agent that can build and change a whole product end to end.

elements.name: Model calls for tests and prototypes
elements.what: Where prototype, test and eval runs get their model calls: subscription plans, never per-token API keys.
elements.open: Open-weights models on a local machine (Ollama, llama.cpp): free and weaker, for offline checks
elements.closed: The Claude subscription through `claude -p` (Claude Code run from a script) or a Claude Code routine in the cloud; a ChatGPT plan through Codex CLI (`codex exec`), included in every ChatGPT plan; a Google AI plan through Gemini CLI (higher limits on Pro and Ultra)
elements.pick: `claude -p` on a Claude subscription for every prototype, test and eval; `codex exec` on a ChatGPT plan as the second pool and a second opinion; a per-token API key only for a customer's live work, and only when the owner says yes
elements.why: A plan is a flat fee, so a test run costs nothing extra, and one rule covers every coding harness: draw on the credits the plan includes. Nothing uses an API key unless the owner asks.

elements.name: Code host
elements.what: Its repository, reviews and history.
elements.closed: GitHub
elements.pick: GitHub
elements.why: One place for the code, reviews and history; Forgejo if the entity ever self-hosts.

elements.name: Code review
elements.what: Reviewing what agents write, at the speed they write it.
elements.open: PR-Agent (MIT), now run by its community, no longer by Qodo
elements.closed: CodeRabbit, Greptile, Claude Code review
elements.pick: Claude Code review on every pull request
elements.why: When agents write the code, review, not writing, is the limit.

elements.name: Design tools
elements.what: Mock-ups and design review before building.
elements.closed: Figma
elements.pick: Figma with the entity's design tokens; Google Stitch for quick prototypes
elements.why: Design review before building saves rework.

components.name: Hosting and delivery
components.what: Where the surfaces run and how a change reaches them.

elements.name: Hosting
elements.what: Where the web app and services run.
elements.closed: Vercel
elements.pick: Vercel
elements.why: Each change merged to the main branch goes live; build once per verified batch.

elements.name: Continuous integration
elements.what: Tests and checks on every push.
elements.closed: GitHub Actions
elements.pick: GitHub Actions
elements.why: It runs beside the code host with no extra account.

components.name: Releases
components.what: Versions, gradual rollout and rolling back.

elements.name: Feature flags
elements.what: Turning features on for some people first.
elements.closed: LaunchDarkly
elements.pick: PostHog feature flags
elements.why: One event stream for flags, analytics and experiments; a flag is how a new version reaches a slice of the work.

elements.name: Versions and rollback
elements.what: Every change to the entity is a version that can be undone.
elements.closed: Versions and canaries inside agent platforms (Microsoft Foundry, AWS AgentCore)
elements.pick: Each version a git commit of the harness, shipped to a slice of work behind a flag, with one-step rollback; the promotion gate is under Evolution
elements.why: The improvement loop depends on it.

elements.name: Support and deprecation policy
elements.what: How long each version of its API, MCP server, CLI and SDK is supported, and how a breaking change is announced.
elements.open: Semantic Versioning (a standard); the Deprecation and Sunset HTTP headers (IETF standards: RFC 9745, March 2025, and RFC 8594); Changesets (MIT, 6.1 million npm downloads a week) to write the changelog
elements.closed: Model and API vendors' published policies: Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice before retiring a public model and dates each active model's earliest retirement
elements.pick: Semantic versions on every door; a breaking change announced in the changelog and in the Deprecation header at least 90 days ahead; the previous major version kept for 12 months, matching the MCP specification's window; the protocol versions each agent serves shown on its record
elements.why: Agents call its doors without reading a blog, so the warning has to travel in the response itself. The CNCF (Cloud Native Computing Foundation) asks graduating projects to publish how long each release is supported, and the MCP specification of 28 July 2026 gave deprecated features 12 months.

elements.name: Stage gates and launch review
elements.what: A written go or no-go before each step up: from made-up cases to real users, from working hours to round-the-clock cover, and before each new customer, checked against a list and signed by the owner and a second person.
elements.open: Google's launch coordination checklist and production readiness review, free in the SRE book; MVSP (Minimum Viable Secure Product) as the security floor
elements.closed: None: a checklist and two signatures
elements.pick: Three gates per product, each a checklist in the repo. Real users: the verifier agrees with people on the held-back cases, business associate agreements signed when it handles health data, the kill switch tested, a service level written, a backup restored once. Round-the-clock: a rota staffed, runbooks written, paging tested, a restore drill timed. Each new customer: a load test, the security questionnaire answered, recovery targets agreed. The entity's record shows the last gate it passed
elements.why: Google's SRE book makes a production readiness review a prerequisite before its SRE team takes responsibility for a service in production, and its launch checklist covers capacity, failover, monitoring, security and rollout. A second signer turns the go or no-go into a check, not one person's call. Gates kept in separate records leave no single place that says a product passed them.

components.name: Monitoring and incidents
components.what: Knowing it broke before a customer does.

elements.name: Errors and crashes
elements.what: Stack traces and crash reports.
elements.open: GlitchTip. Self-hosted Sentry is source-available (Functional Source License), not open source
elements.closed: Sentry
elements.pick: Sentry
elements.why: A widely used default; scrub personal data before any event leaves.

elements.name: Uptime and status page
elements.what: Checks from outside and a public status page.
elements.closed: Better Stack, Pingdom, Atlassian Statuspage
elements.pick: Better Stack: the checks, a public status page and phone alerts, which an agent sets up and reads through its hosted MCP server or API; Uptime Kuma, self-hosted, where a company must run its own
elements.why: The test is whether an agent can use it on its own. Better Stack has a hosted MCP server with tools for monitors, incidents and status pages and a supported API; it is free for personal projects and $29 a month per responder, billed yearly, for a business. Uptime Kuma, the open runner-up, has only an internal API its project does not support, so an agent reaches it only through the screen; ntfy carries phone alerts where Uptime Kuma runs.

elements.name: On-call and incidents
elements.what: Who is woken, and the write-up after.
elements.closed: PagerDuty, incident.io
elements.pick: A written runbook and a phone alert at first; incident.io once there is a rota and a paying customer
elements.why: For an agent an incident is usually a wrong action, not downtime, so the kill switch matters more than paging. Google's SRE book sets response times of 5 minutes for user-facing services and 30 for others.

elements.name: Service levels
elements.what: A written promise of response and correction times, with a remedy when they are missed.
elements.closed: Set inside the support tool (Zendesk, Fin)
elements.pick: Targets per grade, measured from the inbox and shown on the record page
elements.why: A regulated buyer needs a written remedy before it signs.

components.name: Cost control
components.what: Budgets per agent, and what each outcome costs.

elements.name: Compute budgets
elements.what: Spend per agent against its grade, in near real time.
elements.closed: Anthropic task and session budgets, OpenRouter limits per key
elements.pick: A server-side stop at the grade's compute cap
elements.why: A dashboard warning is not a cap.

components.name: Backups and recovery
components.what: Getting back what was lost.

elements.name: Backups
elements.what: Copies of data and memory, tested by restoring them.
elements.closed: Supabase backups with point-in-time recovery, AWS Backup
elements.pick: Supabase backups for records, restic for memory and files, git for every harness
elements.why: A backup counts only once it has been restored; test one every quarter.

elements.name: Disaster recovery and failover
elements.what: Bringing the service back after a region, a provider or the database fails: written recovery targets, a standby and practised drills.
elements.open: CloudNativePG (Apache 2.0, 9,367 stars) and Patroni (MIT, 8,749) for Postgres failover; Velero (Apache 2.0, 10,315) to restore whole clusters
elements.closed: Supabase point-in-time recovery; AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery for whole servers
elements.pick: Written recovery targets per customer before any real customer data; a restore drill each quarter that brings one whole agent back on a fresh machine (harness from git, memory from restic, records from point-in-time recovery) and times it; a model provider outage pauses judgement work and resumes it, never a quiet switch to a weaker model; a second region only when a contract asks
elements.why: Backups bring back data; only a practised restore brings back the service. Google's launch checklist asks what happens when a machine, rack or cluster fails, SOC 2's availability criteria cover disaster recovery and continuity plans, and a health system's security questionnaire asks for both.

components.name: Lifecycle
components.what: Starting, moving and retiring an agent.

elements.name: Onboarding
elements.what: Hiring an agent into a workspace with its contract.
elements.closed: Microsoft Entra Agent ID and Okta for AI Agents (identity at hire)
elements.pick: An agent platform that hires each agent into a workspace with a written contract
elements.why: A contract at hire is enough until an enterprise asks for its own identity system; then map it to Entra or Okta.

elements.name: Stack provisioning
elements.what: Creating a new company's software accounts (hosting, database, analytics, errors) in one step.
elements.closed: Stripe Projects (generally available; 49 providers)
elements.pick: Stripe Projects where the provider is on it, with the keys moved straight into the secrets keeper (Trust: Security), never left in files; for every other provider a person does the one-time sign-up, card or code, and the agent finishes through the provider's MCP server or CLI
elements.why: The accounts land in the company's own name, each provider bills at its own rate, and the command line suits agents. Stripe Projects lists 49 providers; for the rest the split is the same: a person does each one-time step and the agent does everything after it.

elements.name: Handoff and retirement
elements.what: Moving its work, memory and record when it changes owner or stops.
elements.closed: None worth naming
elements.pick: Handoff moves the record and memory to a new owner; retirement revokes every key, exports the memory and record, and archives
elements.why: Stopping an agent is one action (Trust: Kill switch); a handoff also needs its memory and record exported, handed to the new owner and archived.

elements.name: Agent inventory and access reviews
elements.what: One roster of every agent it runs, with its owner, grants and status, and a review of each grant on a schedule.
elements.open: None built for agents leads; Backstage's software catalogue (Apache 2.0, 34,513 stars) can list agents beside services
elements.closed: Microsoft Agent 365 (one registry of every agent; generally available 1 May 2026 at $15 per user a month); AWS AgentCore Registry
elements.pick: A registry per organisation listing each agent's owner, grants and last review date; every grant reviewed each quarter and at every change of owner, and unused grants removed; mirrored into Agent 365 when a customer runs Microsoft
elements.why: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework asks for an inventory of AI systems (GOVERN 1.6), and an unreviewed grant is how an agent ends up with more access than its job. A roster alone is not enough: each grant also needs its scheduled review.

elements.name: Bring-up order
elements.what: The order of a new company's one-time human steps, and how long each takes, so the slow ones start first.
elements.closed: None: a checklist
elements.pick: Start every slow step on day one, in this order: formation and the tax number (the same day online with a US Social Security number, 4 to 8 weeks by fax without one); the bank account and the card issuer's identity checks, and Ramp's early access; the texting registration (one to two weeks) and Meta's business verification; the postal address (USPS Form 1583); then everything that needs only a key, the same day (Operations: Provisioning)
elements.why: Identity checks and one-time codes gate everything after them and take days, so a company that starts them last waits weeks with nothing to show; each step's own row holds its detail.

components.name: Workspaces
components.what: The container its agents live in, one per person or company.

elements.name: Workspaces and tenancy
elements.what: Keeping each customer's agents, data and bills apart.
elements.open: Database rules that keep each customer's rows apart (Supabase row-level security), Keycloak
elements.closed: Clerk Organizations, WorkOS
elements.pick: An organization per customer in the sign-in layer, with the database keeping each customer's rows apart
elements.why: The agent is the unit and the workspace the container; no memory is shared across customers.

elements.name: Deployment modes
elements.what: Its own cloud, the buyer's cloud, or sealed off on open-weight models; what stays separate per customer and what is shared on purpose.
elements.closed: Claude Managed Agents with self-hosted workers, AWS Bedrock AgentCore
elements.pick: The entity's own cloud first; the buyer's cloud when a contract asks
elements.why: A security team asks four things first: separation, revocation, what it can reach, and whether its data trains a model.

elements.name: One account per company
elements.what: Whether each company gets its own account with each provider, and how its keys are kept apart from every other company's.
elements.closed: Providers' own sub-accounts, for example AgentMail's pods
elements.pick: One account or sub-account per company with each provider (its own payments account, phone sub-account, inbox pod, database project and code organisation), under the operator's master accounts where the provider offers them, with one scoped key per entity held by the keeper; keys never cross companies
elements.why: Each company's payments account and texting brand carry its own tax number, and a leaked key must reach one company only.

categories.name: Evolution
categories.question: How does it get better on its own?
categories.what: The signals it learns from, the loop that turns them into proven changes under a written contract, lessons shared across the fleet, and the search for what should exist next. Every feature ships with its trace and its eval so this can attach.

components.name: Signals
components.what: Where the evidence of right and wrong comes from.

elements.name: Correction capture
elements.what: Capturing every edit, redo and override a person makes to the work, as data.
elements.closed: LangSmith, Braintrust feedback
elements.pick: Every edit captured in the trace beside the draft it changed
elements.why: The richest signal is the edit a person had to make anyway.

elements.name: Product analytics
elements.what: What people did with the product: accepted, redid, ignored, left.
elements.closed: Amplitude, Mixpanel
elements.pick: PostHog
elements.why: Product analytics, flags and replays in one open-source tool.

elements.name: Asking people
elements.what: Surveys and conversations that say why people did what the numbers show.
elements.closed: Typeform, Tally
elements.pick: PostHog surveys in the product; a weekly session with the person at a design partner who uses it most
elements.why: Numbers say what happened; people say why.

elements.name: Agent usage
elements.what: Which agents call its API, MCP server and CLI, and whether their calls succeed.
elements.closed: None leads
elements.pick: A PostHog event on every call from an agent
elements.why: Agents are users now, and their failed calls are feedback too.

elements.name: Expert labels
elements.what: The answers from the review queue (Trust: Verification) and experts' grades of hard cases, kept as labelled cases.
elements.open: None leads: a plain labelled-case format kept beside the traces
elements.closed: Labelling services: Scale AI, Surge AI, Mercor
elements.pick: Every expert answer saved as a labelled case in the pool
elements.why: The verifier is the scarce part, and its answers become the pool.

elements.name: Failures and incidents
elements.what: Every failure or incident, turned into a test case.
elements.open: Langfuse datasets built from failed traces
elements.closed: Braintrust, LangSmith datasets
elements.pick: Each incident written up and added to the held-back cases
elements.why: A failure fixed without a test comes back.

elements.name: Outside signals
elements.what: What the market, the press and the owner's saved posts say.
elements.closed: Meltwater, Brandwatch
elements.pick: An ingestion pipeline that turns outside sources into notes the entity can search
elements.why: What the market says reaches the entity as searchable notes, and the same notes give the improvement loop new challenges (Evolution: New challenges).

elements.name: Physical-world signals
elements.what: Sensors, devices and events off the screen.
elements.closed: Samsara, AWS IoT
elements.pick: Readings from the sensors chosen under Physical world, read-only by default
elements.why: A machine completes work only under a rule the buyer approved in advance.

elements.name: Business outcomes
elements.what: The real result of each job (the test happened, the invoice was paid, the case was closed), logged with a reason and joined to its trace.
elements.open: PostHog (MIT outside its enterprise folder) events, or Langfuse scores on the trace
elements.closed: Paid (billing on agent outcomes; $21 million raised, led by Lightspeed); outcome-priced vendors such as Fin record each resolution as the billable event
elements.pick: Each job's outcome read back from the system of record a set time after the job (for example kept, cancelled or no-show; paid or unpaid) with a reason code; a daily report shows it beside the verified score, and the improvement loop stops when the score rises while outcomes do not
elements.why: A verifier can be satisfied while the customer never arrives. The outcome is the anchor against gaming the metric, the first of the four ways an improvement loop fails (Evolution: Guardrails).

components.name: Improvement loop
components.what: Proposals, gates, promotion and rollback, every night.

elements.name: Self-improvement contract
elements.what: A manifest saying what may change, how each change is tested and how it is undone, with a level a tool verifies.
elements.open: None published: a manifest file kept in the repository
elements.closed: None: managed harnesses wrap their own loops (Microsoft, AWS)
elements.pick: A written self-improvement contract in the repository, graded from level 0 (evals exist) and 1 (evals gate merges) to 2 (a scheduled loop proposes changes) and 3 (the loop improves itself), aiming at level 3
elements.why: A level that is verified by a tool, never asserted, is the difference between a claim and a loop.

elements.name: Loop engine
elements.what: The loop itself: review, propose, validate, ship, archive and invent the next objective, run by an improver separate from the doer.
elements.open: RRSI (a September 2026 Google Research method for improving harnesses), Stanford's Meta-Harness, AutoAgent
elements.closed: Microsoft Agent Optimizer, AWS AgentCore recommendations
elements.pick: An improver separate from the doer, following RRSI's rules, run in E2B
elements.why: The improver never grades its own work, and it runs in a sandbox branched from production.

elements.name: Proposals
elements.what: Candidate changes to prompts, skills, tools and rules.
elements.open: GEPA (a method that improves prompts by reflecting on past runs) with DSPy; the karpathy/autoresearch loop
elements.closed: Google AlphaEvolve (open to all Google Cloud customers since 9 July 2026)
elements.pick: GEPA against the entity's held-back cases; the autoresearch loop for cheap metrics
elements.why: GEPA beat reinforcement learning by 6 percent on average with up to 35 times fewer trial runs.

elements.name: Selection
elements.what: Which candidates survive: ranked by performance and novelty, with a noise floor and a cost rule.
elements.closed: None found
elements.pick: Performance and novelty together, with a noise floor
elements.why: Extra tokens must buy measured gain, and parts that stop helping are pruned.

elements.name: Promotion gates
elements.what: A change ships only if held-back cases improve.
elements.closed: None: nobody sells harness self-improvement
elements.pick: A gate that promotes a change only when held-back cases improve, with the loop's level (0 to 3) verified by a tool
elements.why: Three guards from the September 2026 papers: evolve on tasks kept apart from the evals you report, change one module at a time, and reject extra tokens that buy no gain.

elements.name: Guardrails
elements.what: Limits on the loop itself: no self-merge, a cost budget per run, no secrets in its context.
elements.closed: None found
elements.pick: A person merges every change, and the loop never sees a secret
elements.why: It guards against the four ways a loop fails: gaming the metric, a wrong target, loops fighting each other, and measurements drifting from reality.

elements.name: Signal vetting
elements.what: Verifying where each correction, memory and lesson came from, and whether it is sound, before it trains the agent or spreads to others.
elements.open: cleanlab (Apache 2.0, 11,676 stars) to flag suspect labels; Argilla (Apache 2.0) for a second person's look
elements.closed: Input scanners for planted instructions: Lakera Guard (bought by Check Point, September 2025), Protect AI (bought by Palo Alto Networks, July 2025)
elements.pick: Every correction, memory and lesson carries its source (who, which case, when) and waits in quarantine until it passes a rule check, an injection scan for anything from outside (Trust: Prompt-injection defence) and, for a correction that would change a rule, a second expert; a cap on how much any one source can add; a lesson reaches other agents only after it beats the held-back cases
elements.why: Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute found that about 250 poisoned documents could plant a backdoor in models from 600 million to 13 billion parameters, whatever their size (October 2025). OWASP lists data poisoning (LLM04) and memory poisoning (ASI06), and a loop that learns from every correction learns from a bad one too.

components.name: Fleet learning
components.what: One agent's lesson reaches all of them, without moving anyone's data.

elements.name: Job recipes
elements.what: The job's method as data, re-fitted by corrections; it travels between customers, their data never does.
elements.open: None leads: a recipe kept as versioned files
elements.closed: None worth naming
elements.pick: A recipe per job, kept as versioned data and re-fitted by corrections
elements.why: The method can travel between customers; each customer's record and verified cases do not.

elements.name: Lesson propagation
elements.what: Carrying the lesson, never the customer's data.
elements.open: Skill hubs in Hermes Agent and OpenClaw (no gate)
elements.closed: Anthropic's Dreams for Managed Agents memory stores
elements.pick: Lessons shared as versioned skills and rules, each passing a held-back gate
elements.why: The standard travels, the data does not.

components.name: Open-endedness
components.what: Searching for what should exist next, not only improving what exists.

elements.name: Archive of variants
elements.what: Keeping many good-in-a-niche variants as stepping stones.
elements.closed: Google AlphaEvolve
elements.pick: An archive of variants, each kept with the niche it is best at
elements.why: A variant that is best at one niche today can lead somewhere better later.

elements.name: New challenges
elements.what: Harder tasks and new environments, so the loop never runs out of room.
elements.closed: None worth naming
elements.pick: Outside signals (Evolution: Outside signals) turned into new challenges for the loop
elements.why: Jeff Clune's third rule of open-ended search: generate the environments, not only the solutions.

elements.name: Proposing new jobs
elements.what: Reading the record for work nobody asked for, and proposing it for a person to approve.
elements.closed: None worth naming
elements.pick: The entity proposes; a person approves
elements.why: Reading the record for work nobody asked for is how one contract becomes a company.

components.name: The pool of verified cases
components.what: De-identified verified cases and corrections the entity has written rights to keep.

elements.name: Collection with rights
elements.what: Keeping verified cases as reusable tests and training environments, only where the contract grants it.
elements.open: The verifiers format (Prime Intellect), Hugging Face datasets
elements.closed: Scale AI's data engine
elements.pick: Each held-back verification case written as a test case in Prime Intellect's open format (verifiers)
elements.why: So a case can later test or train a model, and be shared once the rights allow it.

elements.name: De-identification
elements.what: Removing anything that identifies a person before a case is kept.
elements.closed: Google Cloud Sensitive Data Protection, AWS Comprehend Medical, Private AI
elements.pick: The Privacy tool (Presidio), with an expert's spot check before a case is kept
elements.why: Tools catch most identifiers; a person verifies the rest before a case is kept.

components.name: Experiments
components.what: Testing one version against another on live work.

elements.name: A/B tests
elements.what: Two versions of a prompt, skill or page, judged on outcomes.
elements.open: PostHog experiments, GrowthBook, Langfuse prompt versions
elements.closed: Statsig (OpenAI), LaunchDarkly
elements.pick: PostHog experiments with Langfuse prompt versions, judged by the promotion gate
elements.why: One analytics stack; PostHog is already the default under Product analytics.

categories.name: Money
categories.question: How does money come in, go out and get counted?
categories.what: The accounts it holds, pricing, billing, spending, the books and payouts.

components.name: Accounts
components.what: What it holds in its own name: a bank account, a card with a hard cap, a wallet, and a key to get paid.

elements.name: Card with a hard cap
elements.what: A card whose limit the card network enforces.
elements.open: None: card issuing is regulated. The rails are open standards: Visa Intelligent Commerce and Mastercard Agent Pay tokens
elements.closed: Ramp Agent Cards (Visa tokens, MCP and the Ramp CLI), Mercury agent cards (API and CLI), Stripe Issuing for agents, Agentcard (agentcard.sh; MCP and a CLI)
elements.pick: Ramp Agent Cards once Ramp's early access for company-owned agents opens: a single-use card for each purchase, locked to one merchant and one amount, reached over MCP or the Ramp CLI. Until then, Mercury agent cards for recurring charges, with the keeper filling the checkout, and Agentcard's Vault for one owner's own purchases; Stripe Issuing when the company issues cards to its customers' employees under its own brand
elements.why: Ramp costs nothing for the core platform and unlimited virtual cards, and each card is a single-use Visa network token with a hard cap per purchase and every action in Ramp's audit log; company-owned agents are in limited early access, so apply now. Agentcard, the runner-up many agent builders use, is live today with a hosted MCP server, a CLI and a skill, and its Vault also keeps the card from the agent (free up to 5,000 users), but its Issuing, which gives each agent a card of its own, costs $5,000 a month. A Mercury agent reads its card's full number by API; only a person can create one or raise its limit.

elements.name: Bank account
elements.what: Where money lands and is held.
elements.open: None: a bank is a regulated service
elements.closed: Mercury, Meow (run over MCP); Brex now belongs to Capital One
elements.pick: Mercury
elements.why: More than 300,000 customers and a conditional national bank charter (April 2026); Meow is the agent-operable alternative.

elements.name: Crypto wallet
elements.what: A wallet it holds for stablecoin payments.
elements.closed: Coinbase Agentic Wallets (split keys, session caps), Turnkey
elements.pick: Coinbase Agentic Wallets, once a customer pays in stablecoins or an agent trades
elements.why: The keys live with the keeper, never in the agent's environment.

elements.name: Account for getting paid
elements.what: A key that only this entity can use to take payments.
elements.open: None acquires money; Hyperswitch routes payments across card processors
elements.closed: Stripe
elements.pick: Stripe with a restricted key
elements.why: Never the account's main key.

components.name: Pricing
components.what: What a customer pays and for what.

elements.name: Business model
elements.what: What it sells (software, work done as a service, or outcomes) and how it is delivered.
elements.closed: Precedents: Sierra and Fin (formerly Intercom; owned by Salesforce since 10 September 2026) sell outcomes; most AI software sells seats
elements.pick: Sell the outcome, delivered by a forward-deployed team; the shape of the price is decided under Pricing: Price model
elements.why: The order of exposure: sell the outcome first, and any platform behind it later.

elements.name: Price model
elements.what: Priced like a hire: a setup fee, a base at the agent's grade quoted yearly and billed monthly, and a bonus when it beats agreed numbers.
elements.closed: Outcome pricing: Fin (formerly Intercom; owned by Salesforce since 10 September 2026) charges $0.99 per resolved conversation; the Fin agent reached about $110 million a year by April 2026
elements.pick: Priced like a hire
elements.why: A setup fee, a base at the grade and a bonus on agreed numbers; never flat, never uncapped.

components.name: Billing
components.what: Metering usage and outcomes, invoicing and collecting.

elements.name: Metering and invoicing
elements.what: Counting what each agent did and billing it.
elements.closed: Stripe Billing with Metronome, Orb
elements.pick: Stripe Billing meters; one billable event per verified output
elements.why: Build the event, buy the invoice: the verified record is where billing starts.

elements.name: Sales tax and VAT
elements.what: Collecting and filing tax on what is sold.
elements.open: None maintained: tax rates are paid data that change often
elements.closed: Anrok, Stripe Tax, Avalara
elements.pick: Stripe Tax first; Anrok once sales span several states
elements.why: Whether an AI employee is taxable differs by state, so classify it before the first invoice.

elements.name: Merchant of record
elements.what: A reseller that sells on its behalf and carries sales tax and VAT, for products sold to people worldwide.
elements.closed: Paddle, Stripe Managed Payments
elements.pick: Not for invoices to businesses; Polar for a self-serve product sold worldwide
elements.why: A product invoiced business to business needs none. Stripe Managed Payments is the runner-up because it keeps everything in the one Stripe account, but it adds 3.5% on top of Stripe's 2.9% plus 30 cents; Polar is open source, reachable by MCP, CLI, skills and API, and costs 5% plus 50 cents on its free plan (3.8% plus 40 cents at $20 a month). Stripe's ticks here are Stripe as a whole: its MCP server names no Managed Payments tools.

elements.name: Refunds, disputes and collections
