elements.what: Chasing unpaid invoices, retrying failed payments, refunds, and answering card disputes.
elements.open: Lago (AGPL 3.0, 10,627 stars) handles retries and dunning (reminders to pay); Kill Bill (Apache 2.0) has an overdue module
elements.closed: Stripe Billing and Invoicing: reminders, retries of failed payments and dispute handling in the same ledger as the invoice
elements.pick: Stripe Invoicing's reminders and retries; invoices due in 30 days; no charge for a job that failed its verification, so refunds stay rare; a dispute answered with the signed record as evidence; the agent may draft a refund and a person approves it; in health care, never collect patients' debts
elements.why: Billing starts from the verified record (Money: Billing), so the same record settles an argument. Build the meter; buy invoicing, tax and collections.

components.name: Spending
components.what: Controlled spend across vendors and employees.

elements.name: Spend management
elements.what: Cards, receipts and approvals for the company's spending.
elements.closed: Ramp ($44 billion, its last closed round, June 2026), Brex (now Capital One)
elements.pick: Mercury's cards first, from the bank account; the company opens Ramp when its first entity needs a card (Money: Accounts), and spending that needs approvals moves to Ramp then
elements.why: Same login and business check as the bank; one Ramp account then serves both the entities' cards and approvals.

components.name: Books
components.what: Accounting, reporting and the numbers per agent.

elements.name: Accounting
elements.what: The books, closed monthly.
elements.closed: QuickBooks Online, Xero; Rillet and Digits, built on AI
elements.pick: QuickBooks Online kept by an accountant who serves startups; a ledger per agent, built in-house
elements.why: Cost from traces and revenue from Stripe give each agent its own profit and loss; the CPA (Pilot, Kruze) also files the taxes.

elements.name: Treasury
elements.what: Where cash waits, and what it earns while it waits.
elements.closed: Mercury Treasury; Meow (run over MCP)
elements.pick: Only after a raise; until then cash stays in the bank
elements.why: Operating cash needs no yield; a raise does.

elements.name: Reporting
elements.what: Cost, revenue and margin per agent, in the daily brief.
elements.closed: Looker, Tableau
elements.pick: A daily brief built in-house
elements.why: One page a day: cost, revenue and margin per agent.

elements.name: Tax filings
elements.what: Income, franchise and payroll returns, beyond sales tax.
elements.closed: Startup CPAs (certified public accountants) such as Pilot and Kruze, who also claim the research credit; the payroll provider files payroll returns
elements.pick: A startup CPA files the federal return (Form 1120), a Delaware corporation's franchise tax and annual report by 1 March each year on the assumed par value method, and any state tax on the business, such as Washington's business and occupation tax on gross receipts; payroll returns through the payroll provider; the research credit taken against payroll tax while there is no profit
elements.why: Delaware's default method can bill a startup with millions of authorised shares far more than the $400 minimum under the assumed par value method. A qualified small business can apply up to $500,000 a year of research credit to payroll taxes, and since the July 2025 tax law domestic research costs are deducted in the year they are spent.

elements.name: Budget, burn and runway
elements.what: The monthly plan against the actuals: what the company spends, what it earns, and how many months of cash are left, reviewed every month.
elements.open: A spreadsheet or a plain-text ledger (beancount, hledger) with a forecast beside it
elements.closed: The startup CPA's (certified public accountant's) monthly close in QuickBooks Online, with a forecast built on it (Pilot, Kruze)
elements.pick: A monthly budget per line, in this order (compute, accounts, experts, people, trust, growth), against actuals from the monthly close; burn and months of runway in the daily brief; the raise sized from it: months to the next milestone times monthly spend
elements.why: YC's seed guide sizes a round by the months of operation it funds, usually 12 to 18, and says the amount must be tied to a believable plan; investors' data-room lists ask for basic financials including the burn rate. Cost and margin per agent do not show the company's months of cash.

components.name: Payouts
components.what: Paying experts and partners their share.

elements.name: Revenue shares
elements.what: Experts get a share of what the agents they trained earn.
elements.closed: Stripe Connect
elements.pick: Hourly pay at a fair rate, plus a share of what the agents they trained earn, once a lawyer clears it
elements.why: No market standard exists for experts' revenue share, and in health care, payments to clinicians tied to business they can steer are restricted.

categories.name: Growth
categories.question: How do people find it, and why do they stay?
categories.what: Marketing, distribution, sales and support. Marketing buys the first try; only the product keeps a customer.

components.name: Brand
components.what: Its name, look, voice and the page that explains it.

elements.name: Name, look and voice
elements.what: The brand every surface shares.
elements.open: BRAND.md and a shared set of design tokens; Penpot
elements.closed: Figma, Canva
elements.pick: The company's BRAND.md on one shared set of design tokens, used by every surface it sells through
elements.why: One brand for the company and its products on one design system; each agent keeps its own name inside it; buy nothing.

elements.name: Homepage
elements.what: The one page that says what it does and for whom.
elements.closed: Framer ($2 billion, August 2025)
elements.pick: A page in the entity's own Next.js app on Vercel (Software), with no separate site builder
elements.why: A site builder adds a second stack for no gain.

components.name: Content
components.what: What it publishes, and where.

elements.name: Content engine
elements.what: Posts, clips and articles made from real work.
elements.open: Activepieces pipelines (MIT outside its enterprise folder); MoneyPrinterTurbo for short video. n8n is fair-code, not open source
elements.closed: No closed tool leads; many single-purpose tools
elements.pick: The entity's own content agent
elements.why: It drafts from real work, and the owner approves every post before it goes out.

elements.name: Social publishing
elements.what: Scheduling and posting across networks.
elements.closed: Buffer, Hootsuite
elements.pick: Postiz, hosted or self-hosted, posting through each network's official API, with a person approving each post (Reach: Social accounts)
elements.why: The most used open scheduler (36,415 stars), with an MCP server, a CLI and skills for the agent and one queue for every network; Mixpost has slowed.

components.name: Being found
components.what: Search, answer engines, launches and listings.

elements.name: Search engines
elements.what: Showing up in ordinary search results.
elements.open: None leads: the site framework does it (sitemaps, structured data)
elements.closed: Ahrefs, Semrush
elements.pick: Crawlable pages, sitemaps and structured data on the record pages
elements.why: Buy a tool only once organic search becomes a channel.

elements.name: Answer engines
elements.what: Being quoted when people ask ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Perplexity.
elements.open: llms.txt (cheap, but no proven effect on being quoted)
elements.closed: Profound ($1.8 billion, September 2026), Peec AI
elements.pick: Record pages written as the facts answer engines quote; Peec to measure once a page is worth tracking
elements.why: About 10 percent of 300,000 domains publish llms.txt, and no major platform confirms using it.

elements.name: Launches
elements.what: Launch days on the sites builders read.
elements.closed: Product Hunt, Hacker News (Show HN), X
elements.pick: One release at a time from the owner's account; Show HN for developer tools; Product Hunt only for consumer apps
elements.why: A launch speaks in the owner's name, so each post needs the owner's yes.

elements.name: Listings
elements.what: App stores, cloud marketplaces and vendor programmes where people buy.
elements.closed: Epic's app marketplace, AWS Marketplace, Salesforce AgentExchange; Claude's and OpenAI's app directories
elements.pick: Epic's marketplace for a product sold to health systems; the assistants' directories through the MCP App under Surfaces; a cloud marketplace when a buyer asks
elements.why: Epic's marketplace is where health systems look; the reported fee (about $1,900 a year) is not on Epic's public pages, so confirm it before paying.

elements.name: Events
elements.what: Conferences, trade shows and meetups, when they are the best place to meet buyers or builders.
elements.closed: The shows themselves: HIMSS for health IT (Epic reported its agents' results at HIMSS26, March 2026); AGNTCon and MCPCon for agent builders (22 to 23 October 2026, San Jose); Luma to host meetups
elements.pick: One at a time, each once there is something to show: a health IT show once a health product has a record, an agent builders' conference once an open-source release ships; nothing booked without the owner's yes
elements.why: An event costs days of founder time, the scarcest input before the first customer; buyers of health IT and the records vendors meet at HIMSS.

components.name: Community, creators and paid reach
components.what: People who talk about it, and people paid to.

elements.name: Community
elements.what: Where users meet and help each other.
elements.closed: Discord, Circle
elements.pick: Discord for builders first; a public Discourse forum once questions repeat
elements.why: Public threads can be read by search engines, answer engines and agents; a chat server mostly cannot. Discord comes first because the builders are there now; Discourse, which agents can read and act on more (a local MCP server, skills and an llms.txt), follows once questions repeat.

elements.name: Creators
elements.what: Creators paid on results, briefed with real before-and-after clips.
elements.closed: Whop Content Rewards ($0.20 to $6 per 1,000 verified views)
elements.pick: Nothing until retention is proven; then creators paid on results, for builder and consumer products, never for healthcare
elements.why: Coconote reports $6.7 million a year with 10 to 12 specialist creators, by a creator-tool vendor's own account; paying for reach before customers stay wastes it.

elements.name: Ads
elements.what: Paid reach, only once retention is proven.
elements.closed: Meta Advantage+, Google Ads
elements.pick: Nothing until retention is proven; then Meta Advantage+ with the entity's own creative
elements.why: Marketing buys the first try; the product keeps a customer, and support helps it do so. Never an AI actor posing as a clinician or a patient.

components.name: Growth loops
components.what: Growth built into the product.

elements.name: Signed work
elements.what: Every piece of work carries a quiet line saying who did it.
elements.closed: None: a product feature
elements.pick: Built into every agent's output
elements.why: The strongest loop: every finished job advertises to the person who needs the next one.

elements.name: Referrals
elements.what: Customers bringing customers, tracked and rewarded.
elements.closed: Rewardful
elements.pick: The loops built into the product first; Dub for links and attribution
elements.why: Signed work and copying an agent bring the next customer; Dub counts them.

elements.name: Lifecycle email
elements.what: Onboarding and re-engagement email.
elements.closed: Customer.io, Loops, Mailchimp
elements.pick: Product email through the email sender under Software (Resend); a lifecycle tool once a self-serve funnel exists
elements.why: Until a self-serve funnel exists, there is nothing to nurture.

components.name: Sales
components.what: Finding, tracking and closing customers.

elements.name: Customer records (CRM)
elements.what: Every lead, deal and conversation.
elements.closed: Salesforce, HubSpot, Attio
elements.pick: Twenty
elements.why: Open and API-first, so agents read and write every record; with a single design partner, a shared document is enough.

elements.name: Outbound
elements.what: Reaching the right people first.
elements.closed: Clay ($7.1 billion, September 2026) for data; Instantly, Smartlead, Apollo for sending
elements.pick: None where a market runs on referrals; for builder products, only once the ideal customer is proven
elements.why: Outreach speaks in the owner's name, so nothing is sent without the owner's yes.

elements.name: Partnerships
elements.what: Design partners, the records software the customer already runs, the channels people reach it through, and the compute providers below it.
elements.closed: None: relationships
elements.pick: Four kinds of partner: design partners who shape the product, the records software the customer already runs, the channels people reach the entity through, and the compute providers below it
elements.why: Four kinds, each with a win for both sides.

elements.name: Beachhead and buyer map
elements.what: Which customers it serves first, the job it does for them, and who inside each customer is measured on the result.
elements.closed: None: a decision
elements.pick: One narrow segment and one job its customers name; the buyer is whoever is measured on that job's result; the verifier is the staff member who does the job today; the customer's security review is the gate; the second customer is sold on the first one's record
elements.why: Start where customers name the job and cannot keep up today. Check who else wants it: Epic's own patient agent books appointments, and Assort Health raised $120 million at $1.2 billion in June 2026 for phone agents in specialty practices.

components.name: Support and success
components.what: Helping customers and keeping them.

elements.name: Help desk
elements.what: Answering customers, by agent first and person second.
elements.closed: Fin (formerly Intercom; owned by Salesforce since 10 September 2026), Sierra, Decagon, Zendesk
elements.pick: The entity's own support agent answering in a Chatwoot inbox
elements.why: Fin, Sierra and Decagon price per outcome; they are comparables, not vendors to buy.

elements.name: Customer success
elements.what: Onboarding each customer, watching the account's health and earning the renewal.
elements.closed: Gainsight, Vitally
elements.pick: A weekly proof report per agent; the forward-deployed engineer owns the account
elements.why: The renewal follows the record.

categories.name: People
categories.question: Who stands behind it?
categories.what: A small core team that guards the product, experts at the edge who verify and teach it, and the rules they all work by.

components.name: Core team
components.what: Full-time people who guard the product.

elements.name: Founders and product team
elements.what: The small team that owns the product and its taste.
elements.closed: None: people
elements.pick: The founders, with agent employees doing the build
elements.why: AI-native startups make $2 million to $4 million of revenue per person; the core team guards the product, never contractors.

elements.name: Forward-deployed engineers
elements.what: People who sit with the first customers and turn their work into agent employees.
elements.closed: None: people
elements.pick: First hire, about $160,000 to $220,000 base
elements.why: Agent employees can do the integration half of the week.

elements.name: Maintainers and contributors
elements.what: For an open-source entity: named maintainers from more than one organisation, a contributor ladder and a CONTRIBUTING guide.
elements.open: None: people. The CNCF's graduation criteria and opensource.guide set the practice; all-contributors (MIT) credits every kind of contribution
elements.closed: None: people
elements.pick: From the first public release: a MAINTAINERS file naming at least two people, a CONTRIBUTING guide, and a person who merges every change (agent employees triage and review, never merge); a maintainer from a second organisation before any claim of neutrality
elements.why: The CNCF requires maintainers from at least two organisations and a contributor ladder that produces them. OpenSSF Scorecard gives its top contributor score only to projects with contributors from three companies, each with five of the last 30 commits.

elements.name: People per product
elements.what: Which roles on each product must be people, how many, and at which stage each is filled: the owner, the verifier, the approver, on-call and support. Agents do the rest.
elements.open: None: a plan. Google's SRE book (site reliability engineering, free at sre.google) gives the arithmetic for round-the-clock cover
elements.closed: None: a plan. PagerDuty or incident.io hold the rota once one exists (Operations: On-call and incidents)
elements.pick: One page per product, kept beside its contract and reviewed at every stage gate. Prototype: the founder alone, with the lead verifier paid by the hour. Production: a named owner for each agent, the lead verifier from the customer's staff, the forward-deployed engineer (a founder until the first hire) by day, and a written response time for every hour the product is promised to work. Round-the-clock cover comes from the company's one rota (People: Experts at the edge), with the agent's own first response limited to stopping work. Support: the product's own support agent first, a person for escalations. Revisit the plan when incidents pass two per 12-hour shift
elements.why: Google's SRE book: with a primary and a secondary always on call and at most 25% of each engineer's time on call, a single-site team needs at least 8 people and a dual-site team 6 per site; typical response times are 5 minutes for user-facing services and 30 for less time-sensitive ones; an incident takes about 6 hours of work, so one 12-hour shift can absorb at most two. AI-native startups make $2 million to $4 million of revenue per person (Forbes, 31 March 2026).

components.name: Experts at the edge
components.what: The people whose corrections add knowledge to the system.

elements.name: Employed or contracted experts
elements.what: Specialists paid for verification, per case or per hour.
elements.open: None: people; review screens such as Label Studio
elements.closed: Expert networks, for discovery only (GLG, Guidepoint)
elements.pick: Named experts on direct contracts, paid per hour or per case at an agreed rate
elements.why: The verifier is the scarce part; expert networks teach a new vertical but never verify work.

elements.name: Crowdsourced experts
elements.what: Experts found and paid through a marketplace.
elements.closed: Prolific (self-serve, a public API and an official CLI), Tendem by Toloka (a hosted MCP server), Mercor, micro1, Surge AI, Handshake AI
elements.pick: A marketplace only for overflow reviewers, self-serve and driven by the agent: Prolific first, Tendem by Toloka second, with a person approving every spend; Mercor, micro1 or Surge AI only by contract for a vertical's specialists, after a vendor review
elements.why: They pay experts about $60 to $125 an hour; Scale AI lost its neutrality after Meta's stake. Only Prolific and Tendem are self-serve: Mercor, micro1, Surge AI, Handshake AI, Turing and Invisible sell through sales teams, so an agent reaches them only after a contract (Surge AI then offers an API and an official Python SDK; none of them showed an MCP server or CLI on 27 September 2026). Prolific charges companies a 42.8% platform fee, and publishing a study spends real money at once. Mercor's March 2026 breach came through a compromised open-source library. Prolific comes before Tendem, though Tendem's hosted MCP server is easier to drive, because Prolific is self-serve at a published price (a 42.8% platform fee), where Tendem quotes each task.

elements.name: Approver roster
elements.what: The people who say yes to risky actions.
elements.closed: None: people
elements.pick: The owner named on each agent (Harness: Identity), plus the customer's own approvers
elements.why: People manage the queue of exceptions, not the agents.

elements.name: Cover around the clock
elements.what: Enough people to answer an approval at any hour; agents do not remove this.
elements.closed: PagerDuty schedules
elements.pick: The customer's own staff by day; one rota per company, not per product, once any product works at night, with overnight cover bought if needed
elements.why: An unanswered approval must do nothing, so someone has to be there. Google's SRE book sizes round-the-clock cover at 8 people on one site, or 6 per site on two, with at most two incidents per 12-hour shift; a small company cannot staff that per product.

elements.name: Expert bench per vertical
elements.what: How many experts a vertical needs and where each comes from: a lead verifier, a second rater who measures agreement, and a specialist for escalations, with the sourcing order written down.
elements.open: None: people. Label Studio or Argilla hold the double-labelled cases; agreement is measured with Cohen's kappa for two raters, Fleiss' kappa for three or more
elements.closed: Direct contracts first. Marketplaces for the second rater and overflow: Prolific (self-serve, a 42.8% platform fee for companies, an official CLI and MCP server), Tendem by Toloka (10,000 or more vetted experts reached over MCP), Mercor and micro1 (sales-led, hourly experts), Handshake AI (hourly PhD experts)
elements.pick: At least three named experts per vertical before real work: the lead verifier from the customer's own staff, a second rater who labels the same 200 held-back cases on their own, and a specialist per case for escalations, plus a backup so an approval never waits. Add a rater whenever the weekly review queue exceeds the hours the bench gives. Source in this order: the customer's staff, directly recruited specialists, then a marketplace; expert networks (GLG, Guidepoint) only to learn a new vertical
elements.why: A verifier can only be trusted to agree with people as well as people agree with each other, and measuring that takes two independent raters: many texts set 80% agreement as the minimum, and a kappa below 0.60 means inadequate agreement (McHugh, 2012). Mercor's advertised expert rate averaged $109 an hour on 26 August 2026 and its take is estimated at 30 to 35%, so demand that lasts favours direct contracts.

elements.name: Credential checks
elements.what: Confirming at the source that every expert who signs regulated work holds the licence they claim, before their first sign-off and again before it expires.
elements.open: None: licences are held by state boards. The NPPES registry of US provider numbers is free with an API, but a provider number does not prove a licence
elements.closed: DocInfo (docinfo.org) to verify a doctor's licence, with the Federation of State Medical Boards' data API for volume; Nursys QuickConfirm for nurses, a primary-source equivalent for participating boards; each state bar's lookup for lawyers
elements.pick: Before a person's first sign-off, verify the licence with the issuing board or its designated equivalent (DocInfo for physicians, Nursys for nurses, the state bar for lawyers); keep the licence number, state and expiry on the expert's record and re-check before expiry. An expert whose licence cannot be verified may label cases but never signs
elements.why: The NPPES registry itself says that issuing a provider number does not ensure or validate that the provider is licensed or credentialed. In regulated work a named person stands behind the output (Trust: Expert sign-off), so the name has only as much value as its licence check.

components.name: Advisors
components.what: People who lend judgement and relationships.

elements.name: Advisors
elements.what: Named advisors per vertical.
elements.closed: None: people
elements.pick: Advisors only where they open a door (a health system, a payer)
elements.why: Standard advisor terms come from free templates (the FAST agreement).

components.name: Hiring
components.what: Finding and signing people.

elements.name: Recruiting
elements.what: Finding and tracking candidates.
elements.closed: Ashby, Greenhouse, Gem
elements.pick: The Twenty list (Growth: Sales) until the first hiring push, then Ashby
elements.why: Ashby costs about $400 a month under 100 staff, by one secondary source; ask Ashby for a quote.

elements.name: Contractors and global hiring
elements.what: Paying people in other countries and contractors.
elements.closed: Deel ($49 a month per contractor, $599 per employee abroad), Remote; Upwork
elements.pick: Direct contracts with named people; Deel only for a hire abroad
elements.why: Named people keep the knowledge and the assignment clean.

elements.name: Hiring paperwork and worker classification
elements.what: The legal steps for every person paid: a contract or offer letter, a work-eligibility check for each employee, and a written decision on whether each expert is a contractor or an employee.
elements.open: None: government forms (USCIS Form I-9; IRS Form SS-8 to ask the IRS for a ruling)
elements.closed: The payroll provider files much of it (Gusto, under Pay: Payroll and benefits); Deel as employer of record abroad
elements.pick: Form I-9 completed within three business days of each employee's first day; offer letters and expert contracts that carry the invention assignment (Company: Intellectual property); every expert and contractor classified against the IRS's three kinds of evidence (behavioural control, financial control, the type of relationship) before the first payment, with the reasoning kept; a lawyer reviews any expert who works most weeks for the company
elements.why: USCIS requires Section 2 of Form I-9 within three business days after an employee's first day. The IRS weighs behavioural, financial and relationship facts to decide who is an employee, and a ruling on Form SS-8 can take 6 months. Classification is the live risk in expert work: annotators sued Surge AI in May 2025 and Outlier contractors sued Scale AI over pay, while Handshake hires all its AI fellows as 1099 contractors.

components.name: Pay and incentives
components.what: Salaries, benefits and equity for the people who build it.

elements.name: Payroll and benefits
elements.what: Paying staff and their benefits.
elements.open: Frappe HR, Horilla, OrangeHRM (none files payroll taxes)
elements.closed: Gusto, Rippling, Justworks
elements.pick: Gusto at the first US hire
elements.why: It files payroll taxes for a small US team.

elements.name: Equity and shares
elements.what: Options and shares for the people who build it.
elements.closed: Carta, Pulley
elements.pick: Individual grants from the option plan kept under Company: Governance
elements.why: The plan and the valuation it needs are decided once, under Company.

components.name: Direction
components.what: Deciding what to build next.

elements.name: The daily direction prompt
elements.what: One long prompt a day, turned into rules and to-dos by the harness.
elements.closed: None: a practice
elements.pick: A daily prompt from the owner, kept with its ledgers
elements.why: The owner sets direction once a day; the harness turns it into rules and to-dos.

elements.name: Work tracking
elements.what: The master to-do list people and agents both read.
elements.open: Markdown ledgers in git. claude-task-master adds the Commons Clause (no right to sell), so it is not open source
elements.closed: Linear, Jira
elements.pick: Markdown to-do ledgers in the repo
elements.why: People and agents read the same list.

components.name: Workplace tools
components.what: Where the team talks and writes.

elements.name: Team chat
elements.what: Where the team and its agents talk.
elements.closed: Slack, Microsoft Teams
elements.pick: Slack
elements.why: Many tools connect to it, and agents join as themselves.

elements.name: Documents and knowledge
elements.what: Where the team writes things down.
elements.closed: Notion, Google Docs, Confluence
elements.pick: The same Markdown the agents read (Shared knowledge, under Harness)
elements.why: One source for people and agents, read as a website.

elements.name: Video calls
elements.what: Where the team and its customers meet by video, and where an entity's meeting bot joins them.
elements.closed: Google Meet (in Google Workspace), Microsoft Teams, Zoom
elements.pick: Google Meet, included in the Google Workspace the staff sign in with (video meetings for up to 100 people on the entry plan); a customer's Teams or Zoom when the meeting is theirs, joined by the entity through Recall.ai (Reach: Meetings)
elements.why: When Workspace is the one staff sign-in (Trust: Staff access), Meet adds no cost. A company that sells into Microsoft customers may run Teams instead.

components.name: Operating rules and team measures
components.what: How work is run, written once so nobody repeats it.

elements.name: Standing rules
elements.what: The owner's standing patterns and the repo's rule files.
elements.closed: None worth naming
elements.pick: A checklist of the owner's standing rules, kept in the repo
elements.why: A correction said three times becomes a rule, so nobody has to say it a fourth time; the rule files agents load are under Harness: Identity.

elements.name: Team metrics
elements.what: Revenue per person and the ratio of people to agents; the cost and revenue per agent come from Money: Books.
elements.closed: None: a practice
elements.pick: Both numbers in the daily brief
elements.why: Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index made the ratio of people to agents a business measure.

elements.name: Training
elements.what: AI literacy and security training for everyone who works with the agents: founders, engineers and experts at the edge.
elements.open: None as software; free material: the European Commission's AI literacy questions and answers, and OWASP's top 10 lists for LLM and agent applications
elements.closed: Security awareness platforms such as KnowBe4; the training modules inside compliance tools such as Vanta and Drata
elements.pick: One hour at onboarding and once a year, recorded per person: what the agents may and may not do, how to spot and stop a wrong action, and prompt injection; with health data, also handling patient data, and HIPAA security training before anyone touches it; run through the compliance tool so the auditor sees the record
elements.why: The EU AI Act has required AI literacy for staff since 2 February 2025 (the Digital Omnibus on AI, in force 27 July 2026, softened it to supporting literacy). HIPAA's Security Rule requires training all workforce members, and it applies to business associates. NIST asks the same (GOVERN 2.2).

categories.name: Company
categories.question: What legal body does it live in?
categories.what: Forming the company, governing it, its legal papers, its intellectual property and its insurance. A named person still has to stand behind it.

components.name: Formation
components.what: Creating the legal entity.

elements.name: Legal body and state
elements.what: A Delaware C-corp or an LLC, formed and kept in good standing.
elements.closed: Stripe Atlas, doola (a Formation API with an MCP server), Clerky, Firstbase, Naive
elements.pick: A Delaware C-corp if it may ever raise, an LLC only if it earns and never raises; formed through Stripe Atlas, or through doola's Partner API when a parent company forms many companies (doola's hosted MCP server forms Wyoming LLCs only)
elements.why: Venture rounds and the QSBS tax exclusion (no federal tax on gains from qualifying small-company stock) need C-corp stock, and a priced seed round buys preferred stock in a corporation. doola sells formation to platforms by its Partner API, for LLCs and C-corps in any US state; its hosted MCP server, with a person paying at checkout and signing the IRS forms, covers Wyoming LLCs only as of 27 September 2026. Naive retired its post naming doola, and its page (7 September 2026) no longer names its provider.

elements.name: Registered agent
elements.what: The address that receives legal papers.
elements.closed: Included by the formation service in the first year
elements.pick: Whatever the formation service includes
elements.why: It only has to receive legal papers reliably.

elements.name: Tax registration (EIN in the US)
elements.what: The tax number: the IRS's EIN in the US, a VAT or GST number elsewhere. It needs a named person.
elements.closed: IRS
elements.pick: Filed with the founder as responsible party
elements.why: No vendor removes the named person, and the IRS issues one tax number per responsible person per day, which paces a fleet of agent-run companies.

elements.name: Registration where it works
elements.what: Registering where the team works (a US state; elsewhere, the local register), with its tax accounts.
elements.closed: The state itself; formation services can file it
elements.pick: Register in each state where the team works
elements.why: A Delaware company working in another state must register there too.

elements.name: Agent-run company
elements.what: A company an agent manages rather than a person.
elements.closed: Wyoming's DAO LLC (a company whose rules can be run by software); MIDAO in the Marshall Islands
elements.pick: Watch only
elements.why: The tax number and the bank's identity check still need a named person.

elements.name: Foundation or fiscal host
elements.what: The legal home of a project with no company: a foundation that holds its name and process, or a fiscal host that holds its money.
elements.open: Open Source Collective, a fiscal host (about 10 percent of incoming money; its platform is MIT); Linux Foundation homes such as the Agentic AI Foundation, which hosts MCP, AGENTS.md and goose
elements.closed: None: foundations are non-profits; the alternative is a company that owns the project
elements.pick: A company's own projects stay in the company; a standard meant for others to adopt moves to a Linux Foundation home once outside companies depend on it; Open Source Collective for a project that needs only somewhere to hold money
elements.why: Agent standards are moving to neutral homes: the Agentic AI Foundation formed on 9 December 2025 and the x402 Foundation on 2 April 2026. Neutrality is what gets competitors to adopt a standard, and it also hands over control.

elements.name: Licences and permits
elements.what: Licences for regulated activities, per place, beyond forming the company.
elements.closed: The state, county and city themselves; formation and compliance services can file and track renewals
elements.pick: A state business licence and any city endorsement where the team works; no money transmitter licence while a processor such as Stripe and the card issuer hold and move the money, never the entity; a licence check per vertical before an agent takes a licensed job, such as collecting debts
elements.why: The SBA (Small Business Administration) says most businesses need a mix of federal and state licences that depend on the activity and the place, and some expire. An agent that takes on a licensed job inherits that job's licence.

components.name: Governance
components.what: Who decides, and who owns what.

elements.name: Board and bylaws
elements.what: The operating agreement or bylaws, and the board.
elements.open: Free standard documents (Series Seed, the venture industry's NVCA models)
elements.closed: Stripe Atlas's Cooley documents, Clerky
elements.pick: A founders-only board until a priced round; the formation service's standard documents, such as Atlas's, read once by a lawyer
elements.why: SAFE (a simple agreement for future equity, the usual first investment) holders get no seat or vote before their SAFE converts.

elements.name: Decision records
elements.what: Rules and decisions kept append-only and changed only by proposal, with one page of what waits on the owner.
elements.closed: None worth naming
elements.pick: Decision records in git, with one questions file that lists what waits on the owner
elements.why: A decision nobody can find gets made twice.

elements.name: Cap table and equity plan
elements.what: Who owns what, and the option plan.
elements.closed: Carta (Pulley shuts down on 8 December 2026)
elements.pick: Carta from the first share, reached over its hosted MCP server; keep an Open Cap Format export
elements.why: File the 83(b) election (a tax filing that fixes the founders' shares at today's value) within 30 days of founder stock, and get a 409A valuation (an independent value for the shares) before the first option. Pulley shuts down on 8 December 2026 and moves its customers to Carta, and it had no API, CLI or MCP server; Carta's Launch plan is free up to 25 stakeholders and $1M raised, with a hosted MCP server and official Claude plugins.

elements.name: Project governance and code of conduct
elements.what: For an open project: who decides and how, written down, and the behaviour expected of everyone who takes part.
elements.open: Contributor Covenant (a standard code of conduct used by over 40,000 projects, including Kubernetes, Rails and Swift); a GOVERNANCE file
elements.closed: None: a practice
elements.pick: Contributor Covenant from the first public release, with a named person who handles reports; a GOVERNANCE file saying the founder decides until outside maintainers join, then maintainers decide by consensus with a vote as the fallback
elements.why: The CNCF asks graduating projects for discoverable governance, a written way decisions are made and a code of conduct. A project that writes this before its first dispute does not have to settle it in public.

elements.name: Exit and wind-down
elements.what: Selling, merging or closing in order: the board's decision, notices, final taxes, and customers' data handed back.
elements.closed: None: a legal process, run by the lawyer and the CPA (certified public accountant); Carta publishes the steps for a Delaware company
elements.pick: Written before it is needed: every customer contract says how its agents wind down and how records and memory are exported; with patient data, the business associate agreement requires returning or destroying it with no copies kept; a closing follows a board resolution, IRS Form 966, a Delaware certificate of dissolution and final returns
elements.why: HHS's sample business associate agreement requires returning or destroying all patient data when the agreement ends, for any reason. A buyer's continuity questions ask what happens to its work if the entity stops.

elements.name: Terms with the parent company
elements.what: Who owns each company a parent company forms, what it may use of the parent's harness, recipes and verified cases, what shared services it pays for, and its named responsible person.
elements.closed: None: a contract, drafted once by counsel and reused
elements.pick: One standard agreement per company, signed when it is formed: the parent's stake; a licence, never a transfer, to use the parent's harness, recipes and pool of verified cases while the company runs on them; the shared services it pays for at a stated price; its named responsible person; and what the company owns outright (its customers, its records and what it builds for them)
elements.why: A seed investor checks that the company owns, or may keep using, everything it needs: the data room holds the invention assignments (Funding: Raising), while the parent keeps the harness and the verified cases (Company: Intellectual property). The tax-number rule, one per responsible person per day, also paces how fast a parent can form companies.

components.name: Legal
components.what: The contracts it works under.

elements.name: Terms and privacy policy
elements.what: The public terms, privacy policy and data processing terms.
elements.closed: Law firms; Termly and Iubenda for policies
elements.pick: Common Paper as the first draft, reviewed by a lawyer
elements.why: Free and standard, with data processing terms and an AI addendum.

elements.name: Contracts and signatures
elements.what: Customer contracts, signed electronically.
elements.open: Common Paper drafts; Documenso and DocuSeal for signatures
elements.closed: DocuSign, Ironclad
elements.pick: Common Paper drafts signed in Documenso; the customer's DocuSign when they send one
elements.why: Every customer contract carries the data rights and an AI addendum.

elements.name: Lawyer
elements.what: A lawyer for the first vertical, on a flat fee.
elements.closed: Law firms; AI drafting (Harvey, Spellbook)
elements.pick: A flat-fee lawyer who knows the vertical; with health data, a healthcare lawyer
elements.why: A flat fee keeps the first legal work at a known price; with health data, the lawyer must know HIPAA.

components.name: Intellectual property
components.what: What it owns, and what it gives away.

elements.name: Assignment and trademarks
elements.what: Work assigned to the company; names protected.
elements.closed: Formation services include founders' assignment
elements.pick: Assignment from every founder, hire, contractor and expert; a trademark search before a name is filed
elements.why: Experts' corrections become training data, so their work must be assigned.

elements.name: Open-source licence
elements.what: The licence for what the entity gives away.
elements.closed: Business source licences (source-available, not open)
elements.pick: Apache 2.0, once the owner decides to open the code
elements.why: Apache 2.0 is open and carries a patent grant, while a business source licence is only source-available. When to open the code is the owner's decision.

elements.name: What to open and what to keep
elements.what: What stays the entity's own when the rest is copied or given away.
elements.closed: None: a decision
elements.pick: Give away the method; keep the record, the verified cases, the verifiers and the experts
elements.why: Code copies in a week; data, trust and relationships do not.

elements.name: Contributor agreements
elements.what: How outside contributors confirm they have the right to give their work: a sign-off on each commit or a signed agreement.
elements.open: Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO, a standard: a Signed-off-by line on each commit), checked by the DCO app (ISC); CLA Assistant (Apache 2.0) where a signed contributor licence agreement (CLA) is needed
elements.closed: None: a legal agreement; law firms draft custom CLAs
elements.pick: The DCO with Apache 2.0 and no CLA: Apache 2.0 already carries a patent grant, and a CLA mostly buys the right to relicense, which contributors distrust; commits written by agent employees are signed off by the person who directed them, never by the agent
elements.why: Node.js dropped its CLA for the DCO. The Linux kernel's 2026 rules for AI coding assistants say only a person can certify the DCO, so an agent must never add a Signed-off-by line.

components.name: Insurance
components.what: Cover for the risks it carries.

elements.name: Cyber and errors insurance
elements.what: Cover for breaches and mistakes.
elements.closed: Vouch, Embroker, Corgi
elements.pick: Quotes from Vouch or Embroker and from Corgi, checked against any minimum insurer rating in the customer's contract
elements.why: $3,000 to $20,000 a year for a technology company, broker's range.

elements.name: Cover for AI agents
elements.what: Insurance written for what AI agents do.
elements.closed: AIUC; Armilla (backed by Lloyd's, up to $25 million)
elements.pick: A quote at the first paid contract
elements.why: The first policies written for agents are in use; ElevenLabs insured its voice agents this way.

elements.name: Employer and general liability cover
elements.what: Workers' compensation and the other cover the law requires once there are staff, plus general liability.
elements.closed: Startup packages from Vouch, Embroker and Corgi (Corgi raised $160 million at $1.3 billion on 6 May 2026 and says seed startups often pay $2,000 to $5,000 a year)
elements.pick: General liability in the same package as cyber and errors cover, at the limits the customer's contract names; workers' compensation from the first employee, bought from the state fund where private insurers cannot sell it (in Washington, Labor and Industries)
elements.why: The SBA lists workers' compensation, unemployment and disability insurance as required once a business has employees. Washington is one of four states where workers' compensation comes only from the state fund or self-insurance.

categories.name: Funding
categories.question: Who pays until it pays for itself?
categories.what: Revenue first, then money that costs no ownership, then equity or debt, raised only once one agent employee earns more than it costs.

components.name: Self-funding and customers
components.what: Paying for itself, and customers who invest.

elements.name: Founders pay
elements.what: The founders pay until the first round, within set usage limits.
elements.closed: None: a decision
elements.pick: Founders pay until the first round
elements.why: It costs no ownership; charge the first customer for a pilot.

elements.name: Customers as investors
elements.what: The first customer in a vertical invests alongside the founders.
elements.closed: Precedent: health systems invested in Hippocratic AI
elements.pick: Keep as an option, after a lawyer's review (in healthcare, a healthcare lawyer's)
elements.why: Payments tied to referrals are restricted in healthcare.

components.name: Money without equity
components.what: Credits, grants and accelerators.

elements.name: Startup credits
elements.what: Cloud and model credits.
elements.closed: Anthropic, Google (up to $350,000), AWS (up to $200,000), Microsoft
elements.pick: Apply right after the first outside investment
elements.why: About $1.4 million is available and about $110,000 of it usable on tokens; the large tiers need an institutional investor or accelerator first.

elements.name: Grants and accelerators
elements.what: Grants and programmes that fund without a price.
elements.closed: NIH SBIR grants; Y Combinator
elements.pick: With a health product, an application for an NIH small-business research grant (SBIR); an accelerator is optional
elements.why: SBIR was reauthorized for five years in April 2026 and costs no equity, but takes months.

elements.name: Sponsors and fiscal hosts
elements.what: Money for an open-source project that has no company behind it.
elements.closed: GitHub Sponsors
elements.pick: Only if the entity is an open-source project
elements.why: A project can hold and spend money through a fiscal host without forming a company.

components.name: Equity
components.what: Selling part of the company.

elements.name: Seed round
elements.what: The first priced or SAFE round.
elements.closed: Carta, Clerky, AngelList to sign and hold it
elements.pick: A post-money SAFE (a simple agreement for future shares) with a cap for the first investment; then a priced seed round, valued on contracts already signed
elements.why: 93% of pre-seed rounds were SAFEs in the second quarter of 2026 (Carta).

elements.name: Strategic funds
elements.what: A fund run with a model lab, whose check also opens the lab's credits.
elements.closed: Menlo Ventures' Anthology Fund with Anthropic ($100 million; healthcare in scope)
elements.pick: With Anthropic's models, apply to the Anthology Fund
elements.why: An institutional investment from the lab whose model the entity runs, and it unlocks Anthropic's credits.

elements.name: Community rounds
elements.what: Raising from customers and the public, as many small checks.
elements.closed: Wefunder, Republic, StartEngine: Regulation Crowdfunding allows up to $5 million in 12 months
elements.pick: Skip for business-to-business healthcare; consider it for a consumer agent with fans
elements.why: A public raise adds an offering statement and yearly reports for a sum that is small beside a priced seed, and a health system buys on the record, not on fans; for a consumer product the round doubles as marketing.

components.name: Debt
components.what: Borrowing against revenue.

elements.name: Venture debt and revenue-based financing
elements.what: Loans against revenue or a round.
elements.closed: Lighter Capital, Capchase, Pipe
elements.pick: Not before $200,000 of yearly revenue; later, compute financed against signed contracts
elements.why: Borrow only against contracted cash flow.

components.name: Raising tools
components.what: The data room, the investor list and the updates.

elements.name: Data room and investor updates
elements.what: Sharing documents with investors and reporting monthly.
elements.closed: DocSend
elements.pick: Papermark, with the same Twenty list (Growth: Sales) for investors, design partners and experts. It holds the formation papers, the cap table and every SAFE, founder stock and vesting, the 83(b) elections and invention assignments; at seed add board consents, the equity plan and its 409A, monthly statements, retention, insurance, licences and tax filings
elements.why: One list, three uses. Investors' diligence lists ask for these documents.

elements.name: Deck, summary and metrics
elements.what: What an investor reads first: a one-page summary, a slide deck that stands on its own, and a metrics sheet whose numbers reconcile to the books.
elements.open: YC's seed guide lists the deck's parts (free); slides generated from the record so each number links to its source
elements.closed: Ordinary slide tools; sharing and tracking sit under Data room and investor updates
elements.pick: A one-page summary and a deck in YC's twelve parts (company, vision, problem, customer, solution, market, landscape, traction, business model, team, summary, fundraising), generated from the record: revenue and its growth, retention, gross margin, cost per verified output, revenue per person and people per agent, and a 12 to 18 month plan with its milestones
elements.why: YC's guide says a seed round needs little diligence: an executive summary of one or two pages (vision, product, team, traction, market size, minimum financials) and a deck that works as a leave-behind. Investors' diligence lists ask for monthly financials and revenue detail that reconcile to the traction claims (Hustle Fund).

categories.name: Compute
categories.question: What does it run on, below the waterline?
categories.what: Owning the compute. Rent everything first; go down a layer only when the work already running proves that layer is the bottleneck, across many companies.

components.name: Rented capacity
components.what: Dedicated inference and GPU time from someone else's machines.

elements.name: Dedicated inference
elements.what: Reserved endpoints for the entity's own models.
elements.open: vLLM on rented GPUs; SkyPilot to move between clouds
elements.closed: Fireworks ($17.5 billion, July 2026), Baseten, Together
elements.pick: Together or Nebius on startup credits for simple repeated work; Fireworks once the entity's own tuned models run at volume
elements.why: Over 95 percent of Fireworks' tokens run on models tuned on customers' own data. Together comes first because startup credits cover simple repeated work; Fireworks, a little easier for an agent to drive, follows once the entity's own tuned models run at volume.

elements.name: GPU clouds and neoclouds
elements.what: Renting GPUs by the hour or the month.
elements.closed: CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe, Lambda; RunPod for pods
elements.pick: Nebius through SkyPilot
elements.why: Nebius has the lowest price among the real clouds and no charge to move data out; SkyPilot keeps the work portable across clouds.

elements.name: Serverless GPUs
elements.what: GPUs billed by the second, for bursty jobs.
elements.closed: Modal ($4.65 billion at its last closed round, May 2026; 0.88 seconds to start at the median)
elements.pick: Modal for bursty open-model and fine-tuning jobs
elements.why: Pay by the second; its credits cover the first experiments.

components.name: Serving and training software
components.what: The software that runs and trains models on those machines.

elements.name: Inference engine
elements.what: Serving open models fast.
elements.open: vLLM, SGLang, NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM (Apache 2.0), llama.cpp, Ollama (Hugging Face's TGI is archived)
elements.closed: The engines inside Fireworks and Baseten
elements.pick: vLLM by default; SGLang for agent traffic that repeats long prompts
elements.why: SGLang reuses the shared start of long prompts, so repeated calls cost less; Ollama or llama.cpp on laptops.

elements.name: Training stack
elements.what: The software that runs training on the entity's own machines or rented ones; which model is trained is decided under Intelligence.
elements.closed: Thinking Machines Tinker, OpenAI and Fireworks fine-tuning
elements.pick: Tinker for the first small model; Unsloth or TRL as the portable path
elements.why: Trained only on verified cases the entity has written rights to keep.

components.name: Edge
components.what: Models that run on the person's device or near them.

elements.name: On-device and edge models
elements.what: Small models on phones, laptops and nearby servers, for speed, privacy or no network.
elements.closed: Apple Foundation Models, Gemini Nano
elements.pick: Only when a surface must work offline or in the room
elements.why: Rented models answer everything else for less.

components.name: Own clusters
components.what: Machines the entity owns and schedules.

elements.name: Cluster orchestration
elements.what: Scheduling work across the entity's own GPUs.
elements.closed: Anyscale (agreed to be bought by a neocloud, 30 July 2026), NVIDIA Run:ai
elements.pick: Kubernetes with SkyPilot
elements.why: A portable design: Kubernetes schedules the owned GPUs, and SkyPilot moves the same work across clouds.

components.name: Custom silicon
components.what: Chips built for one kind of work.

elements.name: Chips
elements.what: General GPUs, or chips built for a fixed job.
elements.open: None: AMD's software is open, NVIDIA's CUDA is not
elements.closed: NVIDIA, AMD; Google TPU and AWS Trainium inside their clouds; Groq, Cerebras, Etched, Taalas
elements.pick: Rent only; Groq or Cerebras through their APIs when speed matters for a job
elements.why: Custom silicon paid off only for one frozen workload at huge volume (Anthropic's TPUs; Jane Street with Etched). Hardware would be a consequence of scale, never a starting strategy.

components.name: Data centres and power
components.what: Buildings, land and electricity.

elements.name: Data centres
elements.what: Buildings, cooling and the halls the machines sit in.
elements.closed: Equinix, Digital Realty; GPU-first builders such as Crusoe
elements.pick: Rent through a neocloud; build nothing
elements.why: Owning a building pays only once running work proves it is the bottleneck; the edge is in running compute well, not in owning it.

elements.name: Power
elements.what: Electricity and the grid connection behind every data centre.
elements.closed: Utilities; grid-flexibility sellers such as Emerald AI
elements.pick: Build nothing; track value per token and per megawatt
elements.why: Power is scarce on time, not supply: a heavy gas turbine ordered in 2026 arrives in 2031, and grid queues run four to seven years.

elements.name: Electricity and carbon reporting
elements.what: The electricity use and emissions of the compute it runs on, estimated and reported.
elements.open: CodeCarbon (MIT, 32,835 downloads a week) for compute the entity runs itself; Cloud Carbon Footprint (Apache 2.0) for cloud bills
elements.closed: The clouds' own carbon dashboards; Google publishes 0.24 watt-hours and 0.03 grams of carbon dioxide equivalent for its median Gemini text prompt (August 2025)
elements.pick: Later: an estimate per agent from its token counts and the providers' published figures, added to the owner's daily brief when a customer or a law asks
elements.why: NIST's framework asks for environmental impact to be assessed (MEASURE 2.12), but nothing requires it at small scale, and rented model calls can only be measured by their providers.
